arXiv:0811.0751v1 [math.GR] 05 Nov 2008

Parabolic subgroups of Garside groups II : ribbons

Eddy GODELLE
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

We introduce and investigate the ribbon groupoid associated with a Garside group. Under a technical hypothesis, we prove that this category is a Garside groupoid. We decompose this groupoid into a semi-direct product of two of its parabolic subgroupoids and provide a groupoid presentation. In order to established the latter result, we describe quasi-centralizers in Garside groups. All results hold in the particular case of Artin-Tits groups of spherical type.

1. Introduction

In 1969, Garside solved the conjugacy problem in the braid group by investigating the monoid of positive braids [13]. At the end of the 90’s, Dehornoy and Paris introduced in [10] the notion of a Garside group, that captures most of the properties used in Garside approach. After this seminal paper, the notion has been extended and numerous articles have dealt with Garside monoid/group structures ([2],[7],[8],[17],[22] for instance). Actually various groups can be equipped with a Garside group structure. Recently, Krammer [20], Bessis [3] and Digne-Michel [11] have extended the notion of a Garside group into the notion of a Garside groupoid, which turned out to be crucial in the proof of the long-standing question of the K⁡(π,1)K(\pi,1) property for complex reflection arrangements [3].

The standard examples of Garside groups are braid groups and their generalization, the so-called Artin-Tits groups of spherical type. One of the main properties of Artin-Tits groups is the existence of a family of distinguished subgroups, namely the standard parabolic subgroups, which are the subgroups generated by a subset of the standard generating set. In order to describe normalizers of such subgroups, we were naturally led in [14] (see also [15]) to introduce a groupoid called the ribbon groupoid. In an unpublished paper [11] Digne and Michel prove that the ribbon groupoid of an Artin-Tits group of spherical type is a Garside groupoid. Actually, this result implicit in [16], even though the notion of a Garside groupoid had not been introduced yet. In [17], we extended the notion of a parabolic subgroup into the framework of Garside groups. Our objective here is to go further and extend the notion of ribbon groupoid. We prove that in the context of Garside groups, ribbon groupoids remain a Garside groupoids. Indeed we prove (see next sections for definition) that

Theorem 1.1.

For every Garside group AA with a ν\nu-structure, the positive ribbon category ℛ+​(A+)\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})} is a Garside category and the ribbon groupoid ℛ⁡(A)\mathop{\mathcal{R}\!(A)} is the associated Garside groupoid.

Every Artin-Tits group of spherical type has a ν\nu-structure. Then, Theorem 1.1 applied in this special case. In order to prove Theorem 1.1, we consider the category ⟨𝒞⟩\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle of subcategories of a category 𝒞\mathcal{C}, whose morphisms are natural transformations. It turns out that for a Garside category 𝒞\mathcal{C}, the category ⟨𝒞⟩\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle is not a Garside category in general. However, this category shares nice properties with Garside monoids (see Section 2 for precise definition and results). We also provide a groupoid presentation of the ribbon groupoid ℛ⁡(A)\mathop{\mathcal{R}\!(A)} for every Garside group AA with a ν\nu-structure. To obtain this presentation we investigate the quasi-centralizer Q​Z​(A)QZ(A) of AA, that is the subgroup of AA made of those elements that permute the atoms of the monoid A+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}. In particular we generalize a result of Picantin [22]:

Theorem 1.2.

For every Garside group AA, the group Q​Z​(A)QZ(A) is a finitely generated free commutative group.

Furthermore, we describe the normalizer of the standard parabolic subgroups by proving (see Theorem 4.25):

Theorem 1.3.

Let AA be a Garside group. Let C​o​n​j​(A)Conj(A) be the groupoid whose objects are the parabolic subgroups AXA_{X} of AA, whose Hom-set from AXA_{X} to AYA_{Y} is {g∈A∣g−1​AX​g=AY}\{g\in A\mid g^{-1}A_{X}g=A_{Y}\}, and whose composition is the product in AA. Let 𝒫⁡(A)\mathcal{P}(A) be the totally disconnected groupoid whose objects are the parabolic subgroups of AA and whose vertex group at AXA_{X} is AXA_{X}. Then, there exists a standard parabolic subgroupoid ℛν​(A)\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle\nu}\!(A)} of ℛ⁡(A)\mathop{\mathcal{R}\!(A)} such that C​o​n​j​(A)Conj(A) is equal to the semi-direct product of groupoids 𝒫(A)⋊ℛν​(A)\mathcal{P}(A)\rtimes\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle\nu}\!(A)}.

This theorem generalizes [15, Prop. 4.4]. Finally, the subgroups of the vertex groups of the ribbon groupoid ℛ⁡(A)\mathop{\mathcal{R}\!(A)} that are generated by the atoms contained in the vertex group are Garside groups. This result is similar to [6, Theorem B], which deals with Coxeter groups.

The reader may wonder what is the interest of proving that ribbon groupoids are Garside groupoids. The main point is that it provides a complete description of the connection between standard parabolic subgroups. The notion of a parabolic subgroup is crucial to build important tools like the so-called Deligne complexes of Artin-Tits groups. Therefore to understand their normalizers and their mutually conjugating elements is certainly crucial. Furthermore the fact that ribbon groupoids are Garside groupoids shows that, even in order to study classical groups such as braid groups, the notion of a Garside groupoid is natural and useful. Finally, our groupoid presentations of ribbon groupoids of spherical type Artin-Tits groups provide Garside groupoids with braid-like defining relations. These groupoids are then special among Garside groupoids and therefore should provide seminal examples of Garside groupoids that are not groups.

The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we introduce the notions of a Garside groupoid and of a parabolic subgroupoid; we investigate the category ⟨𝒞⟩\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle. In Section 3, we introduce the positive ribbon category associated with a Garside category and prove Theorem 1.1. Finally, in Section 4 we provide a groupoid presentation of the ribbon groupoid; along the way we prove Theorem 1.2. We conclude with the proof of Theorem 1.3.

2. Garside groupoids

Here we set the necessary terminology on small categories. In particular we recall the notion of a natural transformation between two functors. we introduce the central notion of a Garside groupoid and provide examples.

2.1. Small category

The present paper deals with categories, but the reader should not be scared since we only consider small categories. Let us introduce the notion of a small category and some basic notions in a naive way.

A quiver Γ\Gamma is a pair (V,E)(V,E) of sets equipped with two maps s:E∪V→Vs:E\cup V\to V and t:E∪V→Vt:E\cup V\to V such that s⁡(v)=t⁡(v)=vs(v)=t(v)=v for every element vv of VV. The elements of VV are called the vertices and the elements of EE are called the edges. An edge ee is said to be oriented from its source s⁡(e)s(e) to its target t⁡(e)t(e). The path semigroup ℳ⁡(Γ)\mathcal{M}(\Gamma) associated with the quiver Γ\Gamma is the semigroup with 00 defined by the presentation whose generating set is V∪EV\cup E and whose defining relations are s⁡(e)​e=e=e​t​(e)s(e)e=e=e\,t(e) for every ee in V∪EV\cup E and v1​v2=0v_{1}v_{2}=0 for every two distinct elements of VV. Clearly, we can identify the elements of E∪VE\cup V with their images in ℳ⁡(Γ)\mathcal{M}(\Gamma). Note that a product e1⋯eke_{1}\cdots e_{k} of edges is not equal to 00 in ℳ⁡(Γ)\mathcal{M}(\Gamma) if and only if for every index ii, one has t⁡(ei)=s⁡(ei+1)t(e_{i})=s(e_{i+1}). If ee lies in ℳ⁡(Γ)\mathcal{M}(\Gamma) and is not 00, then one can define its source and its target to be s⁡(e1)s(e_{1}) and t⁡(ek)t(e_{k}) for any of its decomposition e1⋯eke_{1}\cdots e_{k} as a product of elements in V∪EV\cup E. The reader may note that the semigroup algebra of ℳ⁡(Γ)\mathcal{M}(\Gamma) is equal to the path algebra of the quiver Γ\Gamma as defined in [1]. An element of ℳ⁡(Γ)\mathcal{M}(\Gamma) distinct from 00 is called a path in the sequel.

Now, let Γ\Gamma be a quiver and let ≡\equiv be a congruence on ℳ⁡(Γ)\mathcal{M}(\Gamma) such that 00 is alone in its equivalence class 0¯\underline{0} and such that two distinct ≡\equiv-equivalent paths in ℳ⁡(Γ)\mathcal{M}(\Gamma) have the same source and the same target. We denote by ℳ⁡(Γ,≡)\mathcal{M}(\Gamma,\equiv) the quotient semigroup of ℳ⁡(Γ)\mathcal{M}(\Gamma) by the congruence ≡\equiv. By assumption on ≡\equiv, to each equivalence classes of paths e¯\underline{e} one can associate a source and a target by setting s⁡(e¯)=s⁡(e)s(\underline{e})=s(e) and t⁡(e¯)=t⁡(e)t(\underline{e})=t(e), respectively. The (small) category 𝒞⁡(Γ,≡)\mathcal{C}(\Gamma,\equiv) associated with the quiver Γ\Gamma and the congruence ≡\equiv is the set ℳ⁡(Γ,≡)−{0¯}\mathcal{M}(\Gamma,\equiv)-\{\underline{0}\} of non-zero equivalence classes of paths equipped with the source and target maps, and the partial product induced by the product in ℳ⁡(Γ,≡)\mathcal{M}(\Gamma,\equiv). In that context, the vertices of Γ\Gamma are called the objects of the category, and the elements of the category are called the morphisms of the category. The free category 𝒞⁡(Γ)\mathcal{C}(\Gamma) on Γ\Gamma is obtained by considering the trivial congruence.

In the sequel, we denote by V⁡(𝒞)V(\mathcal{C}) the set of objects of a category 𝒞\mathcal{C}. For every xx in V⁡(𝒞)V(\mathcal{C}), we denote by 1x1_{x} the equivalence class of the trivial path xx. For xx and yy in V⁡(𝒞)V(\mathcal{C}), we denote by 𝒞x→y\mathcal{C}_{x\to y} the set of morphisms from xx to yy. In order to be consistent with [8, 3] and with the above naive definition of a small category, if vv lies in 𝒞x→y{\mathcal{C}}_{x\to y} and ww lies in 𝒞y→z\mathcal{C}_{y\to z}, then we denote by v​wvw the morphism of 𝒞x→z\mathcal{C}_{x\to z} obtained by composition. We denote by 𝒞x→⋅\mathcal{C}_{x\to\cdot} and by 𝒞⋅→x\mathcal{C}_{\cdot\to x} the set of morphisms of the category 𝒞\mathcal{C} whose source and target, respectively, are xx. The seminal example to keep in mind is the case of a category with one object xx: this is just a monoid whose unity is 1x1_{x}.

2.2. Functor and natural transformation

Here we introduce the notion of a natural transformation which is crucial in our article. A map Φ:𝒞→𝒞′\Phi:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}^{\prime} from a category 𝒞=𝒞⁡(Γ,≡)\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{C}(\Gamma,\equiv) to a category 𝒞′=𝒞(Γ′,≡′)\mathcal{C}^{\prime}=\mathcal{C}(\Gamma^{\prime},\equiv^{\prime}) is a functor if, firstly, there exists a map ϕ:V⁡(𝒞)→V⁡(𝒞)\phi:V(\mathcal{C})\to V(\mathcal{C}) such that Φ⁡(1x)=1ϕ⁡(x)\Phi(1_{x})=1_{\phi(x)} for every vertex xx in V⁡(𝒞)V(\mathcal{C}) and, secondly, one extends Φ\Phi to a morphism of semigroups from ℳ⁡(Γ,≡)\mathcal{M}(\Gamma,\equiv) to ℳ(Γ′,≡′)\mathcal{M}(\Gamma^{\prime},\equiv^{\prime}) by setting Φ⁡(0¯)={0¯}\Phi(\underline{0})=\{\underline{0}\}. Note that the second property is equivalent to say that Φ⁡(𝒞x→y)\Phi(\mathcal{C}_{x\to y}) is included in 𝒞ϕ⁡(x)→ϕ⁡(y)′\mathcal{C}^{\prime}_{\phi(x)\to\phi(y)} for every two objects x,yx,y of 𝒞\mathcal{C}, and Φ⁡(v​w)=Φ⁡(v)​ϕ​(w)\Phi(vw)=\Phi(v)\phi(w) for every two morphisms ww, vv of 𝒞\mathcal{C} such that t⁡(v)=s⁡(w)t(v)=s(w). For instance, for every category 𝒞⁡(Γ,≡)\mathcal{C}(\Gamma,\equiv), there is a surjective functor from the free category 𝒞⁡(Γ)\mathcal{C}(\Gamma) to 𝒞⁡(Γ,≡)\mathcal{C}(\Gamma,\equiv). An isomorphism of categories is a functor that is bijective. In that case, the inverse is also an isomorphism of categories and the set Φ⁡(𝒞x→y)\Phi(\mathcal{C}_{x\to y}) is equal to 𝒞Φ⁡(x)→Φ⁡(y)\mathcal{C}_{\Phi(x)\to\Phi(y)}. An automorphism of 𝒞\mathcal{C} is an isomorphism from 𝒞\mathcal{C} to itself.

Let 𝒞=𝒞⁡(Γ,≡)\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{C}(\Gamma,\equiv) and 𝒞′=𝒞(Γ′,≡′)\mathcal{C}^{\prime}=\mathcal{C}(\Gamma^{\prime},\equiv^{\prime}) be two categories with Γ=(V,E)\Gamma=(V,E). Let Φ\Phi and Ψ\Psi be two functors from 𝒞\mathcal{C} to 𝒞′\mathcal{C^{\prime}}. Then, a natural transformation Δ\Delta from Φ\Phi to Ψ\Psi is a map Δ:V→𝒞′\Delta:V\to\mathcal{C}^{\prime} that sends every vertex xx in VV to a morphism Δ⁡(x)\Delta(x) from Φ⁡(x)\Phi(x) to Ψ⁡(x)\Psi(x) such that for every two objects x,yx,y in Γ\Gamma and every morphism vv in 𝒞x→y\mathcal{C}_{x\to y}, one has Δ⁡(x)​Ψ​(v)=Φ⁡(v)​Δ​(y)\Delta(x)\Psi(v)=\Phi(v)\Delta(y) (see Figure 1).

For instance, if 𝒞\mathcal{C} and 𝒞′\mathcal{C}^{\prime} are groups and Φ\Phi, Ψ\Psi are two morphisms of groups from 𝒞\mathcal{C} to 𝒞′\mathcal{C}^{\prime}, then a natural transformation from Φ\Phi to Ψ\Psi is an element δ\delta of the group 𝒞′\mathcal{C}^{\prime} such that Ψ⁡(h)=δ−1​Φ​(h)​δ\Psi(h)=\delta^{-1}\Phi(h)\delta for every hh in 𝒞\mathcal{C}.

2.3. Garside groupoid

To introduce the central notion of a Garside groupoid, we need first to fix some definitions.

The atoms of a category 𝒞⁡(Γ,≡)\mathcal{C}(\Gamma,\equiv) are the non-identity morphisms whose representing paths are edges only. The atom graph 𝒜⁡(Γ,≡)\mathcal{A}(\Gamma,\equiv) of the category is the graph that has the same set of vertices than Γ\Gamma and whose edges are the atoms of the category. We recall that a binary relation (defined on a set) is noetherian when every decreasing infinite sequence stabilizes. We say that a morphism ww of 𝒞⁡(Γ,≡)\mathcal{C}(\Gamma,\equiv) is a factor of the morphism w′w^{\prime} when there exist two morphisms w1w_{1} and w2w_{2} such that w′=w1​w′​w2w^{\prime}=w_{1}w^{\prime}w_{2}. We say that the category 𝒞⁡(Γ,≡)\mathcal{C}(\Gamma,\equiv) is noetherian if the set of morphisms is noetherian for factors, in other words, if for every infinite sequence (wi)i∈ℕ(w_{i})_{i\in\mathbb{N}} of morphisms such that wi+1w_{i+1} is a factor of wiw_{i}, there exists an index NN such that wi=wNw_{i}=w_{N} for every i≥Ni\geq N. In this case, the category is atomic: each morphism can be written as a finite product of atoms; furthermore,the category 𝒞⁡(Γ,≡)\mathcal{C}(\Gamma,\equiv) is isomorphic to 𝒞(𝒜(Γ,≡),≡′)\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{A}(\Gamma,\equiv),\equiv^{\prime}), where ≡′\equiv^{\prime} is the congruence on 𝒞⁡(𝒜⁡(Γ,≡))\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{A}(\Gamma,\equiv)) induced by the congruence ≡\equiv. This property holds in particular when for every morphism there is a bound on the lengths of its representing paths in the quiver Γ\Gamma (where each edge has length 11). If in the category 𝒞⁡(Γ,≡)\mathcal{C}(\Gamma,\equiv) there is no loop for the factor relation, then for every object xx the left-divisibility and the right-divisibility induce partial orders on the sets 𝒞x→⋅\mathcal{C}_{x\to\cdot} and 𝒞⋅→x\mathcal{C}_{\cdot\to x}, respectively. This is the case when the category is noetherian. We say that the category 𝒞⁡(Γ,≡)\mathcal{C}(\Gamma,\equiv) is cancellative when for every two objects xx, yy and every morphism vv in 𝒞x→y\mathcal{C}_{x\to y} the maps w↦v​ww\mapsto vw and w↦w​vw\mapsto wv are injective on the sets 𝒞y→⋅\mathcal{C}_{y\to\cdot} and 𝒞⋅→x\mathcal{C}_{\cdot\to x}, respectively.

Finally, a groupoid is a category 𝒞\mathcal{C} such that every morphism has an inverse, in other words, such that for every morphism vv in 𝒞x→y\mathcal{C}_{x\to y} there exists a morphism v~\tilde{v} in 𝒞y→x\mathcal{C}_{y\to x} with v​v~=1xv\tilde{v}=1_{x} and v~​v=1y\tilde{v}v=1_{y}. To each category 𝒞=𝒞⁡(Γ,≡)\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{C}(\Gamma,\equiv) one can associate a groupoid 𝒢⁡(𝒞)=𝒞⁡(Γ~,≡~)\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{C})=\mathcal{C}(\tilde{\Gamma},\tilde{\equiv}) and a functor ι:𝒞→𝒢⁡(𝒞)\iota:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{C}) in the following way. The quiver Γ~\tilde{\Gamma} is obtained by adding to Γ\Gamma an edge v~\tilde{v} from t⁡(v)t(v) to s⁡(v)s(v) for each edge vv of Γ\Gamma. The congruence ≡~\tilde{\equiv} is the congruence generated by ≡\equiv and the relations v​v~=1xv\tilde{v}=1_{x} and v~​v=1y\tilde{v}v=1_{y} for each edge vv from xx to yy in Γ\Gamma. We call the groupoid 𝒢⁡(𝒞)\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{C}) the groupoid of formal inverses of 𝒞\mathcal{C}. For instance, the free groupoid on Γ\Gamma is the groupoid 𝒢⁡(𝒞⁡(Γ))\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{C}(\Gamma)). It should be noted that every functor F:𝒞→𝒟F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D} between two categories induces a functor 𝒢⁡(F):𝒢⁡(𝒞)→𝒢⁡(𝒟)\mathcal{G}(F):\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{C})\to\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{D}) such that the diagram

𝒞↪F𝒟ι𝒞↓ι𝒟↓𝒢⁡(𝒞)↪𝒢⁡(F)𝒢⁡(𝒟)\begin{array}[]{lcl}\ \ \ \mathcal{C}&\stackrel{{\scriptstyle F}}{{\hookrightarrow}}&\ \ \ \mathcal{D}\\ \iota_{\mathcal{C}}\downarrow&&\iota_{\mathcal{D}}\downarrow\\ \ \mathcal{G}(\mathcal{C})&\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{G}(F)}}{{\hookrightarrow}}&\ \mathcal{G}(\mathcal{D})\end{array}

is commutative. We are now ready to introduce the definition of the special kind of groupoids we consider in this paper. We refer to [19] for the general theory on lattices. In [3], Bessis defines the notion of a Garside category as follows.

Definition 2.1 (Garside category).

A categorical Garside structure is a pair (𝒞,Δ)(\mathcal{C},\Delta) such that:

  • •

    𝒞\mathcal{C} is a small category equipped with an automorphism Φ\Phi such that Δ\Delta is a natural transformation from the identity functor I​d:𝒞→𝒞Id:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C} to Φ\Phi;

  • •

    𝒞\mathcal{C} is noetherian and cancellative;

  • •

    for every object xx of 𝒞\mathcal{C}, the sets 𝒞x→⋅\mathcal{C}_{x\to\cdot} and 𝒞⋅→x\mathcal{C}_{\cdot\to x} are lattices for the left-divisibility order and the right-divisibility order, respectively;

  • •

    for every two objects x,yx,y of 𝒞\mathcal{C} and every atom vv in 𝒞x→y\mathcal{C}_{x\to y}, there exists a morphism v¯\overline{v} such that the following diagram is commutative:

In this case, we say that the category 𝒞\mathcal{C} is a Garside category.
We say that (𝒞,Δ)(\mathcal{C},\Delta) is a monoidal Garside structure when furthermore the category 𝒞\mathcal{C} has a unique object. In this case, we say that the monoid 𝒞\mathcal{C} is a Garside monoid.

The reader should note that in the above definition, the automorphism Φ\Phi is uniquely defined by Δ\Delta.

Definition 2.2 (Garside groupoid).

A Garside groupoid 𝒢⁡(𝒞)\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{C}) is the groupoid of formal inverses of a Garside category 𝒞\mathcal{C}. When furthermore 𝒞\mathcal{C} is a monoid, then we say that 𝒢⁡(𝒞)\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{C}) is a Garside group.

If 𝒞\mathcal{C} and 𝒞′\mathcal{C}^{\prime} are two categories and Φ\Phi is a functor, then the subset Φ⁡(𝒞′)\Phi(\mathcal{C}^{\prime}) of 𝒞\mathcal{C} has a natural structure of category. We say that such a subset is a subcategory of 𝒞\mathcal{C}. In the sequel, we denote by ι𝒫\iota_{\mathcal{P}} the canonical functor from the subcategory 𝒫=Φ⁡(𝒞′)\mathcal{P}=\Phi(\mathcal{C}^{\prime}) to the category. The reader should note that, by hypothesis, a Garside category 𝒞\mathcal{C} verifies the so-called Ore relations and, therefore, the functor ι:𝒞→𝒢⁡(𝒞)\iota:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{C}) is injective. In the sequel we consider 𝒞\mathcal{C} as a subcategory of 𝒢⁡(𝒞)\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{C}). Clearly, the automorphism Φ\Phi extends to an automorphism of 𝒢⁡(𝒞)\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{C}), still denoted by Φ\Phi, and that Δ\Delta extends to a natural transformation from the identity functor I​d:𝒢⁡(𝒞)→𝒢⁡(𝒞)Id:\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{C})\to\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{C}) to Φ\Phi.

Example 2.3.

The seminal case of a Garside groupoid 𝒢⁡(𝒞)\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{C}) occurs when the category has one object xx. In this case, the category 𝒞\mathcal{C} is a Garside monoid and 𝒢⁡(𝒞)\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{C}) is its group of fractions, that is a Garside group ([8, 2]). The element Δ⁡(x)\Delta(x) is called the Garside element of the group 𝒢⁡(𝒞)\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{C}), or of the monoid 𝒞\mathcal{C}. In such a Garside group, a natural transformation from the identity morphism to an automorphism corresponds to an element that realizes this automorphism as an inner automorphism. Braid groups and, more generally, Artin-Tits groups of spherical type are Garside groups which are defined by a group presentation of the type

(*) ⟨S|s​t​s​…⏟ms,t​t​e​r​m​s=t​s​t​…⏟ms,t​t​e​r​m​s;∀s,t∈S,s≠t⟩\langle S|\underbrace{sts\ldots}_{m_{s,t}\ terms}=\underbrace{tst\ldots}_{m_{s,t}\ terms}~;\ \forall s,t\in S,s\not=t\ \rangle

where ms,tm_{s,t} are positive integers greater than 2 with ms,t=mt,sm_{s,t}=m_{t,s}. In this case, the associated Coxeter group, which obtained by adding the relations s2=1s^{2}=1 for ss in SS to the presentation, is finite. If we consider S={s1,…,sn}S=\{s_{1},\ldots,s_{n}\} with msi,sj=3m_{s_{i},s_{j}}=3 for |i−j|=1|i-j|=1 and msi,sj=2m_{s_{i},s_{j}}=2 otherwise, we obtain the classical presentation of the braid group Bn+1B_{n+1} on n+1n+1 strings. In that case, the associated Coxeter group is the permutation group on n+1n+1 elements. If AA is such an Artin-Tits group, and WW is its Coxeter group, then the canonical surjection ι:A→W\iota:A\to W has a canonical section [4, Chap. 4]. If we denote by Δ\Delta the image by that section of the greatest element of WW, then Δ\Delta belongs to the submonoid A+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+} of AA generated by SS, and the associated inner group automorphism induces an automorphism of A+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}. It turns out that the pair (A+,Δ)(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+},\Delta) is a monoidal Garside structure with AA for associated Garside group. A group can be a Garside group for several monoidal Garside structures. For instance, the braid group Bn+1B_{n+1} has the alternative group presentation:

⟨at​s|at​s​ar​q=ar​q​at​s;(t−r)​(t−q)​(s−r)​(s−q)>0at​s​as​r=as​r​at​r=at​r​at​s;t>s>r⟩\left\langle a_{ts}\left|\begin{array}[]{lcl}a_{ts}a_{rq}=a_{rq}a_{ts}&;&(t-r)(t-q)(s-r)(s-q)>0\\ a_{ts}a_{sr}=a_{sr}a_{tr}=a_{tr}a_{ts}&;&t>s>r\end{array}\right.\right\rangle

where n+1≥t≥s≥1n+1\geq t\geq s\geq 1 for the generators at​sa_{ts}, and if Bn+1B​K​L+B^{BKL+}_{n+1} denotes the submonoid of Bn+1B_{n+1} generated by the at​sa_{ts}, and δ=a(n+1)​n⋯a21\delta=a_{(n+1)n}\cdots a_{21}, then the inner group automorphism of Bn+1B_{n+1} induced by δ\delta restricts to an automorphism of Bn+1B​K​L+B^{BKL+}_{n+1}. Again, the pair (Bn+1B​K​L+,δ)(B^{BKL+}_{n+1},\delta) is a monoidal Garside structure with Bn+1B_{n+1} for associated Garside group. This alternative Garside structure is called the dual Garside structure of the braid group. This point of view was generalized by Bessis in [2] to every Artin-Tits groups of spherical type.

Example 2.4.

[2, 21] The free group F2F_{2} on two letters a,ba,b has a presentation

⟨ai,i∈ℤ∣aiai+1=ajaj+1,i,j∈ℤ⟩\langle a_{i},\ i\in\mathbb{Z}\mid a_{i}a_{i+1}=a_{j}a_{j+1},\ i,j\in\mathbb{Z}\rangle

where a0=aa_{0}=a and a1=ba_{1}=b. Let Δ=a0​a1\Delta=a_{0}a_{1}. If we denote by F2+F_{2}^{\scriptscriptstyle+} the submonoid of F2F_{2} generated by the elements aia_{i}, and by Φ\Phi the automorphism of F2F_{2} that sends aia_{i} onto ai+2a_{i+2}, then (F2+,Δ)(F_{2}^{\scriptscriptstyle+},\Delta) is a monoidal Garside structure with group F2F_{2} as the associated Garside group. The automorphism induced by Δ\Delta is Φ\Phi .

We end this subsection with a definition and two properties of Garside groupoids that we need in the sequel. They are immediate generalizations of well-known properties of Artin-Tits groups.

Definition 2.5 (Simple element).

[3, Def. 2.2] Let (𝒞,Δ)(\mathcal{C},\Delta) be a categorical Garside structure and denote by Φ\Phi the automorphism of 𝒞\mathcal{C} induced by Δ\Delta. A morphism vv in 𝒞x→y\mathcal{C}_{x\to y} is simple if there exists v′v^{\prime} in 𝒞y→Φ⁡(x)\mathcal{C}_{y\to\Phi(x)} such that v​v′=Δ⁡(x)vv^{\prime}=\Delta(x).

Note that in the above definition the morphism v′v^{\prime} is also simple. By definition of a Garside category, the atoms are simple.

Proposition 2.6.

Let (𝒞,Δ)(\mathcal{C},\Delta) be a categorical Garside structure.
(i) [3] Every morphism vv that belongs to 𝒞x→y\mathcal{C}_{x\to y} can be decomposed as a product s1⋯sks_{1}\cdots s_{k} of simple elements.
(ii) Let vv lie in 𝒢​(𝒞)x→y\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{C})_{x\to y}. There exist an object zz, a morphism v1v_{1} in 𝒞x→z\mathcal{C}_{x\to z} and a morphism v2v_{2} in 𝒞y→z\mathcal{C}_{y\to z} such that v1v_{1} and v2v_{2} are prime to each other in 𝒞⋅→z\mathcal{C}_{\cdot\to z} and vv is equal to v1​v2−1v_{1}v_{2}^{-1}. The triple (z,v1,v2)(z,v_{1},v_{2}) is unique.

Point (i​i)(ii) of the above proposition does not appear in [3], but the proof is similar to the case of Garside groups. We call the triple (z,v1,v2)(z,v_{1},v_{2}) the right greedy normal form of vv There is a similar unique left greedy normal form v3−1​v4v_{3}^{-1}v_{4}.

2.4. The category of subcategories

Definition 2.7 (Category of subcategories).

Let 𝒞\mathcal{C} be a (small) category. We define the category of subcategories ⟨𝒞⟩\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle of 𝒞\mathcal{C} as follows:

  • •

    the objects are the non-empty subcategories of 𝒞\mathcal{C};

  • •

    if 𝒫\mathcal{P} and 𝒬\mathcal{Q} are two subcategories of 𝒞\mathcal{C}, then δ\delta lies in ⟨𝒞⟩𝒫→𝒬\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle_{\mathcal{P}\to\mathcal{Q}} if there exists an isomorphism ϕ\phi from 𝒫\mathcal{P} to 𝒬\mathcal{Q} such that δ\delta is a natural transformation from ι𝒫\iota_{\mathcal{P}} to ι𝒬∘ϕ\iota_{\mathcal{Q}}\circ\phi.

  • •

    If δ1\delta_{1} and δ2\delta_{2} belong to ⟨𝒞⟩𝒫→𝒬\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle_{\mathcal{P}\to\mathcal{Q}} and ⟨𝒞⟩𝒬→⋅\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle_{\mathcal{Q}\to\cdot}, respectively, then the composition morphism δ1​δ2\delta_{1}\delta_{2} is defined by δ1​δ2​(x)=δ1​(x)​δ2​(ϕ1​(x))\delta_{1}\delta_{2}(x)=\delta_{1}(x)\delta_{2}(\phi_{1}(x)), where ϕ1\phi_{1} is the isomorphism associated with δ1\delta_{1}.

Note that in the second item of Definition 2.7 the isomorphism ϕ\phi is uniquely defined by δ\delta because 𝒞\mathcal{C} is cancellative; in the third item, δ1​δ2\delta_{1}\delta_{2} is a natural transformation from ι𝒫\iota_{\mathcal{P}} to ι𝒬′∘ϕ2∘ϕ1\iota_{\mathcal{Q}^{\prime}}\circ\phi_{2}\circ\phi_{1}, where 𝒬′\mathcal{Q}^{\prime} is such that δ2\delta_{2} belongs to ⟨𝒞⟩𝒬→⋅𝒬′\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle_{\mathcal{Q}\to\cdot\mathcal{Q}^{\prime}}.

Our objective below is to investigate the properties of ⟨𝒞⟩\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle and, in particular, to decide whether or not ⟨𝒞⟩\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle is a Garside category.

Proposition 2.8.

Let (𝒞,Δ)(\mathcal{C},\Delta) be a categorical Garside structure and denote by Φ\Phi the automorphism of 𝒞\mathcal{C} induced by Δ\Delta.
(i) There exist an automorphism ⟨Φ⟩\langle\Phi\rangle of ⟨𝒞⟩\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle and a natural transformation ⟨Δ⟩\langle\Delta\rangle from the identity functor of ⟨𝒞⟩\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle to ⟨Φ⟩\langle\Phi\rangle that are induced by Φ\Phi and Δ\Delta.
(ii) The category ⟨𝒞⟩\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle is cancellative.
(iii) For every object 𝒫\mathcal{P} of ⟨𝒞⟩\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle, the left-divisibility and the right-divisibility define partial orders on ⟨𝒞⟩𝒫→⋅\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle_{\mathcal{P}\to\cdot} and ⟨𝒞⟩⋅→𝒫\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle_{\cdot\to\mathcal{P}}, respectively.

Proof.

(i) Let 𝒫\mathcal{P}, 𝒬\mathcal{Q} be two objects of ⟨𝒞⟩\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle and assume δ\delta lies in ⟨𝒞⟩𝒫→𝒬\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle_{\mathcal{P}\to\mathcal{Q}}; denote by ϕ:𝒫→𝒬\phi:\mathcal{P}\to\mathcal{Q} the isomorphism defined by δ\delta. Then, Φ∘ϕ∘Φ−1\Phi\circ\phi\circ\Phi^{-1} is an isomorphism from Φ⁡(𝒫)\Phi(\mathcal{P}) to Φ⁡(𝒬)\Phi(\mathcal{Q}), and the map Φ∘δ∘Φ−1\Phi\circ\delta\circ\Phi^{-1} is a natural transformation from the canonical embedding ιΦ⁡(𝒫)\iota_{\Phi(\mathcal{P})} to ιΦ⁡(𝒬)∘Φ∘ϕ∘Φ−1\iota_{\Phi(\mathcal{Q})}\circ\Phi\circ\phi\circ\Phi^{-1}. Therefore, we define an isomorphism ⟨Φ⟩\langle\Phi\rangle of ⟨𝒞⟩\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle by setting ⟨Φ⟩​(𝒫)=Φ​(𝒫)\langle\Phi\rangle(\mathcal{P})=\Phi(\mathcal{P}) and ⟨Φ⟩​(δ)=Φ∘δ∘Φ−1\langle\Phi\rangle(\delta)=\Phi\circ\delta\circ\Phi^{-1}. Now, for every object 𝒫\mathcal{P} of ⟨𝒞⟩\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle we denote by ⟨Δ⟩​(𝒫)\langle\Delta\rangle(\mathcal{P}) the restriction of the map Δ\Delta to the subcategory 𝒫\mathcal{P}. Then, ⟨Δ⟩​(𝒫)\langle\Delta\rangle(\mathcal{P}) lies in ⟨𝒞⟩𝒫→⋅\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle_{\mathcal{P}\to\cdot}. Indeed, the map ⟨Δ⟩​(𝒫)\langle\Delta\rangle(\mathcal{P}) is a natural transformation from ι𝒫\iota_{\mathcal{P}} to ιΦ⁡(𝒫)∘Φ𝒫\iota_{\Phi(\mathcal{P})}\circ\Phi_{\mathcal{P}}, where Φ𝒫\Phi_{\mathcal{P}} is the restriction of Φ\Phi to 𝒫\mathcal{P}. Clearly, the map ⟨Δ⟩\langle\Delta\rangle is a natural transformation from the identity functor of ⟨𝒞⟩\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle to ⟨Φ⟩\langle\Phi\rangle.
(ii) The cancellativity of the category ⟨𝒞⟩\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle follows directly from the cancellativity of the category 𝒞\mathcal{C}.
(iii) There is no loop for the factor relation in ⟨𝒞⟩\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle because there is no loop for the factor relation in 𝒞\mathcal{C}. Therefore, ⟨𝒞⟩𝒫→⋅\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle_{\mathcal{P}\to\cdot} and ⟨𝒞⟩⋅→𝒫\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle_{\cdot\to\mathcal{P}} are partially ordered sets for the left-divisibility and the right-divisibility, respectively. ∎

In the sequel, an object xx of a category 𝒞\mathcal{C} such that 𝒞x→⋅=𝒞⋅→x={1x}\mathcal{C}_{x\to\cdot}=\mathcal{C}_{\cdot\to x}=\{1_{x}\} is called a trivial object of the category.

Proposition 2.9.

Let (𝒞,Δ)(\mathcal{C},\Delta) be a categorical Garside structure such that 𝒞\mathcal{C} has no trivial object. The category ⟨𝒞⟩\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle is noetherian if and only if its object set is finite.

Proof.

Assume 𝒞\mathcal{C} has a finite number of objects. Let (δn)n∈ℕ(\delta_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}} be a sequence of morphisms of ⟨𝒞⟩\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle such that for every nn, the morphism δn+1\delta_{n+1} is a factor of the morphism δn\delta_{n}. We denote by ϕn:𝒫n→𝒬n\phi_{n}:\mathcal{P}_{n}\to\mathcal{Q}_{n} the isomorphism defined by δn\delta_{n}. Let (θn)n≥1(\theta_{n})_{n\geq 1} and (ηn)n≥1(\eta_{n})_{n\geq 1} be the sequences of morphisms of ⟨𝒞⟩\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle such that δn=θn+1​δn+1​ηn+1\delta_{n}=\theta_{n+1}\delta_{n+1}\eta_{n+1}, and denote by (ψn)n≥1(\psi_{n})_{n\geq 1} and (ρn)n≥1(\rho_{n})_{n\geq 1} the isomorphisms associated with (θn)n≥1(\theta_{n})_{n\geq 1} and (ηn)n≥1(\eta_{n})_{n\geq 1}, respectively. Then, for every positive integer nn, every object xx of 𝒫n\mathcal{P}_{n} and every morphism vv of 𝒫n\mathcal{P}_{n}, we have ϕn​(v)=ηn+1​(ϕn+1​(ψn+1​(v)))\phi_{n}(v)=\eta_{n+1}(\phi_{n+1}(\psi_{n+1}(v))) and δn​(x)=θn+1​(x)​δn+1​(ψn+1​(x))​ηn+1​(ϕn+1​(ψn+1​(x)))\delta_{n}(x)=\theta_{n+1}(x)\delta_{n+1}(\psi_{n+1}(x))\eta_{n+1}(\phi_{n+1}(\psi_{n+1}(x))). Since 𝒞\mathcal{C} is noetherian, for every object xx of 𝒫0\mathcal{P}_{0}, there exists some integer NxN_{x} such that for every n≥Nxn\geq N_{x}, we have δn(ψn∘⋯∘ψ1(x))=δNi(ψNi∘⋯∘ψ1(x))\delta_{n}(\psi_{n}\circ\cdots\circ\psi_{1}(x))=\delta_{N_{i}}(\psi_{N_{i}}\circ\cdots\circ\psi_{1}(x)). In particular, for every n≥Nn\geq N we have ψn+1(ψn∘⋯∘ψ1(xi))=ψn∘⋯∘ψ1(xi)\psi_{n+1}(\psi_{n}\circ\cdots\circ\psi_{1}(x_{i}))=\psi_{n}\circ\cdots\circ\psi_{1}(x_{i}), θn+1(ψn∘⋯∘ψ1(xi))=1ψn∘⋯∘ψ1(xi)\theta_{n+1}(\psi_{n}\circ\cdots\circ\psi_{1}(x_{i}))=1_{\psi_{n}\circ\cdots\circ\psi_{1}(x_{i})}, ρn+1(ϕn∘ψn∘⋯∘ψ1(xi))=ϕn∘ψn∘⋯∘ψ1(xi)\rho_{n+1}(\phi_{n}\circ\psi_{n}\circ\cdots\circ\psi_{1}(x_{i}))=\phi_{n}\circ\psi_{n}\circ\cdots\circ\psi_{1}(x_{i}) and ηn+1(ϕn∘ψn∘⋯∘ψ1(xi))=1ϕn∘ψn∘⋯∘ψ1(xi)\eta_{n+1}(\phi_{n}\circ\psi_{n}\circ\cdots\circ\psi_{1}(x_{i}))=1_{\phi_{n}\circ\psi_{n}\circ\cdots\circ\psi_{1}(x_{i})}. Let N=max⁡{Nx∣x∈V⁡(𝒫0)}N=\max\{N_{x}\mid x\in V(\mathcal{P}_{0})\}. From the above discussion, it follows that for every n≥Nn\geq N one has 𝒫i=𝒫N\mathcal{P}_{i}=\mathcal{P}_{N}, 𝒬i=𝒬N\mathcal{Q}_{i}=\mathcal{Q}_{N} and δi=δN\delta_{i}=\delta_{N}.
Assume finally that 𝒞\mathcal{C} has an infinite number of objects; denote by (xi)i≥0(x_{i})_{i\geq 0} a sequence of distinct objects of 𝒞\mathcal{C} such that 𝒞x2​i→x2​i+1\mathcal{C}_{x_{2i}\to x_{2i+1}} is not empty for every ii. We fix a morphism viv_{i} in 𝒞x2​i→x2​i+1\mathcal{C}_{x_{2i}\to x_{2i+1}} for each ii. Let 𝒬i\mathcal{Q}_{i} be the subcategory of 𝒞\mathcal{C} whose set of objects is {x2​j∣j≥i}∪{x2​j+1∣j<i}\{x_{2j}\mid j\geq i\}\cup\{x_{2j+1}\mid j<i\} such that 𝒬i\mathcal{Q}_{i} has trivial objects only. Let 𝒬∞\mathcal{Q}_{\infty} be the subcategory whose object set is {x2​j+1∣j≥0}\{x_{2j+1}\mid j\geq 0\} such that 𝒬∞\mathcal{Q}_{\infty} has trivial objects only. Consider δi\delta_{i} the map from the set of objects of 𝒬i\mathcal{Q}_{i} to the morphisms ⟨𝒞⟩\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle that sends x2​jx_{2j} on vjv_{j} if j≥ij\geq i and x2​j+1x_{2j+1} on 1x2​j+11_{x_{2j+1}} otherwise. Let τi\tau_{i} be the map from the objects of 𝒬i\mathcal{Q}_{i} to the morphisms of ⟨𝒞⟩\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle that sends x2​ix_{2i} on viv_{i} and xkx_{k} on 1xk1_{x_{k}} otherwise. Then, δi\delta_{i} clearly belongs to ⟨𝒞⟩𝒬i→𝒬∞\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle_{\mathcal{Q}_{i}\to\mathcal{Q}_{\infty}} and τi\tau_{i} belongs to ⟨𝒞⟩𝒬i→𝒬i+1\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle_{\mathcal{Q}_{i}\to\mathcal{Q}_{i+1}}. By construction, δi=δi+1​τi\delta_{i}=\delta_{i+1}\tau_{i} for every ii. Hense, the category ⟨𝒞⟩\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle is not noetherian.∎

Lemma 2.10.

Consider a categorical Garside structure (𝒞,Δ)(\mathcal{C},\Delta) and denote by Φ\Phi the automorphism of 𝒞\mathcal{C} induced by Δ\Delta. Assume  𝒫\mathcal{P} is an object of 𝒞\mathcal{C} such that ⟨𝒞⟩𝒫→⋅\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle_{\mathcal{P}\to\cdot} is a lattice for the left-divisibility. Assume δ\delta is an atom of the category ⟨𝒞⟩\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle that belongs to ⟨𝒞⟩𝒫→𝒬\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle_{\mathcal{P}\to\mathcal{Q}}. Then, there exists a morphism δ¯\overline{\delta} in ⟨𝒞⟩⟨Φ⟩​(𝒫)→𝒬\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle_{\langle\Phi\rangle(\mathcal{P})\to\mathcal{Q}} such that the following diagram is commutative:

Proof.

Indeed, since δ\delta is an atom, the greatest common divisor of δ\delta and ⟨Δ⟩​(𝒫)\langle\Delta\rangle(\mathcal{P}) is either trivial or equal to δ\delta. But, δ\delta is a non-identity morphism of ⟨𝒞⟩\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle. Therefore, there exists an object xx of 𝒫\mathcal{P} such that δ⁡(x)\delta(x) is not (the identity morphism) xx. This implies that δ⁡(x)∧Δ⁡(x)\delta(x)\!\wedge\!\Delta(x) is not trivial and the claim follows. ∎

Gathering the above results we get:

Corollary 2.11.

Consider a categorical Garside structure (𝒞​Δ)(\mathcal{C}\Delta) whose object set is finite. Assume that for every object 𝒫\mathcal{P} of ⟨𝒞⟩\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle the sets ⟨𝒞⟩𝒫→⋅\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle_{\mathcal{P}\to\cdot} and ⟨𝒞⟩⋅→𝒫\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle_{\cdot\to\mathcal{P}} are lattices for the left-divisibility and the right-divisibility, respectively. Then, the pair (⟨𝒞⟩,⟨Δ⟩)(\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle,\langle\Delta\rangle) is a categorical Garside structure.

Proof.

The category ⟨𝒞⟩\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle is cancellative and noetherian, and for every non empty subcategory 𝒫\mathcal{P} of 𝒞\mathcal{C} the sets ⟨𝒞⟩𝒫→⋅\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle_{\mathcal{P}\to\cdot} and ⟨𝒞⟩⋅→𝒫\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle_{\cdot\to\mathcal{P}} are lattices for the left-divisibility and the right-divisibility, respectively. Furthermore, ⟨Δ⟩\langle\Delta\rangle is a natural transformation from the identity functor of ⟨𝒞⟩\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle to the automorphism ⟨Φ⟩\langle\Phi\rangle, where Φ\Phi is the automorphism of 𝒞\mathcal{C} induced by Δ\Delta. ∎

There is no clear argument to expect that the left/right-divisibilities induce lattice orders in general. However there is one particular case where this property always hold:

Proposition 2.12.

Consider a monoidal Garside structure (𝒞,Δ)(\mathcal{C},\Delta). Then, for every non-empty subcategory 𝒫\mathcal{P} of 𝒞\mathcal{C} the sets ⟨𝒞⟩𝒫→⋅\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle_{\mathcal{P}\to\cdot} and ⟨𝒞⟩⋅→𝒫\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle_{\cdot\to\mathcal{P}} are lattices for the left-divisibility and the right-divisibility.

Proof.

Consider a categorical Garside structure (𝒞,Φ,Δ)(\mathcal{C},\Phi,\Delta) and a subcategory 𝒫\mathcal{P} of 𝒞\mathcal{C}. Let δ1\delta_{1}, δ2\delta_{2} belong to ⟨𝒞⟩𝒫→⋅\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle_{\mathcal{P}\to\cdot}. For every object xx of 𝒫\mathcal{P}, we set δ1∨δ2​(x)=δ1​(x)∨δ2​(x)\delta_{1}\!\vee\!\delta_{2}(x)=\delta_{1}(x)\!\vee\!\delta_{2}(x) and δ1∧δ2​(x)=δ1​(x)∧δ2​(x)\delta_{1}\!\wedge\!\delta_{2}(x)=\delta_{1}(x)\!\wedge\!\delta_{2}(x) (we recall that 𝒞x→⋅\mathcal{C}_{x\to\cdot} is a lattice). Denote by ϕ1\phi_{1} and ϕ2\phi_{2} the isomorphisms associated with δ1\delta_{1} and δ2\delta_{2}, respectively. We denote by ϕ1∨ϕ2​(x)\phi_{1}\!\vee\!\phi_{2}(x) and ϕ1∧ϕ2​(x)\phi_{1}\!\wedge\!\phi_{2}(x) the objects of 𝒞\mathcal{C} such that δ1∨δ2​(x)\delta_{1}\!\vee\!\delta_{2}(x) and δ1∧δ2​(x)\delta_{1}\!\wedge\!\delta_{2}(x) lie in 𝒞⋅→ϕ1∨ϕ2​(x)\mathcal{C}_{\cdot\to\phi_{1}\!\vee\!\phi_{2}(x)} and 𝒞⋅→ϕ1∧ϕ2​(x)\mathcal{C}_{\cdot\to\phi_{1}\!\wedge\!\phi_{2}(x)}, respectively. Let yy be another object of 𝒫\mathcal{P}, and assume there exists vv in 𝒫x→y\mathcal{P}_{x\to y}. Write δ1∨δ2​(x)=δ1​(x)​θ1​(x)=δ2​(x)​θ2​(x)\delta_{1}\!\vee\!\delta_{2}(x)=\delta_{1}(x)\theta_{1}(x)=\delta_{2}(x)\theta_{2}(x) and δ1∨δ2​(y)=δ1​(y)​θ1​(y)=δ2​(y)​θ2​(y)\delta_{1}\!\vee\!\delta_{2}(y)=\delta_{1}(y)\theta_{1}(y)=\delta_{2}(y)\theta_{2}(y). We have the sequence of equalities δ2​(x)​ϕ2​(v)​θ2​(y)=v​δ2​(y)​θ2​(y)=v​δ1​(y)​θ1​(y)=δ1​(x)​ϕ1​(v)​θ1​(y)\delta_{2}(x)\phi_{2}(v)\theta_{2}(y)=v\delta_{2}(y)\theta_{2}(y)=v\delta_{1}(y)\theta_{1}(y)=\delta_{1}(x)\phi_{1}(v)\theta_{1}(y). Since 𝒞x→⋅\mathcal{C}_{x\to\cdot} is a lattice, there exists a unique morphism ϕ1∨ϕ2​(v)\phi_{1}\!\vee\!\phi_{2}(v) in 𝒞ϕ1∨ϕ2​(x)→ϕ1∨ϕ2​(y)\mathcal{C}_{\phi_{1}\!\vee\!\phi_{2}(x)\to\phi_{1}\!\vee\!\phi_{2}(y)} which verifies the equalities ϕ1​(v)​θ1​(y)=θ1​(x)​(ϕ1∨ϕ2)​(v)\phi_{1}(v)\theta_{1}(y)=\theta_{1}(x)(\phi_{1}\!\vee\!\phi_{2})(v) and ϕ2​(v)​θ2​(y)=θ2​(x)​(ϕ1∨ϕ2)​(v)\phi_{2}(v)\theta_{2}(y)=\theta_{2}(x)(\phi_{1}\!\vee\!\phi_{2})(v). Consider the map ϕ1∨ϕ2\phi_{1}\!\vee\!\phi_{2} that sends an object xx of 𝒫\mathcal{P} to ϕ1∨ϕ2​(x)\phi_{1}\!\vee\!\phi_{2}(x) and an edge vv of 𝒫\mathcal{P} to ϕ1∨ϕ2​(v)\phi_{1}\!\vee\!\phi_{2}(v). Then, by the cancellativity property, for every two objects x,yx,y of 𝒫\mathcal{P}, the restriction of this map to 𝒫x→y\mathcal{P}_{x\to y} is injective. In particular, when 𝒫\mathcal{P} has one object, ϕ1∨ϕ2\phi_{1}\!\vee\!\phi_{2} is an isomorphism from the subcategory 𝒫\mathcal{P} to the subcategory ϕ1∨ϕ2​(𝒫)\phi_{1}\!\vee\!\phi_{2}(\mathcal{P}). Assume that 𝒞\mathcal{C} is a monoid, that is a category with one object. Set αi=(ϕ1∨ϕ2)∘ϕi−1\alpha_{i}=(\phi_{1}\!\vee\!\phi_{2})\circ\phi_{i}^{-1} for i=1,2i=1,2. Clearly, the maps x↦θ1​(x)x\mapsto\theta_{1}(x), x↦θ2​(x)x\mapsto\theta_{2}(x) and x↦δ1∨δ2​(x)x\mapsto\delta_{1}\!\vee\!\delta_{2}(x) are natural transformations from ιϕ1​(𝒫)\iota_{\phi_{1}(\mathcal{P})}, ιϕ2​(𝒫)\iota_{\phi_{2}(\mathcal{P})} and ι𝒫\iota_{\mathcal{P}} to ιϕ1∨ϕ2​(𝒫)∘α1\iota_{\phi_{1}\!\vee\!\phi_{2}(\mathcal{P})}\circ\alpha_{1}, ιϕ1∨ϕ2​(𝒫)∘α2\iota_{\phi_{1}\!\vee\!\phi_{2}(\mathcal{P})}\circ\alpha_{2} and ιϕ1∨ϕ2​(𝒫)∘(ϕ1∨ϕ2)\iota_{\phi_{1}\!\vee\!\phi_{2}(\mathcal{P})}\circ(\phi_{1}\!\vee\!\phi_{2}), respectively. Thus, δ1∨δ2\delta_{1}\!\vee\!\delta_{2} is a common multiple of δ1\delta_{1} and δ2\delta_{2} in ⟨𝒞⟩\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle. Now, assume τ\tau is a common multiple of δ1\delta_{1} and δ2\delta_{2} in ⟨𝒞⟩\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle with τ=δ1​τ1=δ1​τ2\tau=\delta_{1}\tau_{1}=\delta_{1}\tau_{2}. Let ψ\psi the isomorphism associated with τ\tau. Then, for every object xx of 𝒫\mathcal{P}, there exists ρ⁡(x)\rho(x) in 𝒞ϕ1∨ϕ2​(x)→τ⁡(x)\mathcal{C}_{\phi_{1}\!\vee\!\phi_{2}(x)\to\tau(x)} such that τ1​(x)=θ1​(x)​ρ​(x)\tau_{1}(x)=\theta_{1}(x)\rho(x) and τ2​(x)=θ2​(x)​ρ​(x)\tau_{2}(x)=\theta_{2}(x)\rho(x). Therefore, the map ρ:x↦ρ⁡(x)\rho:x\mapsto\rho(x) lies in ⟨𝒞⟩(ϕ1∨ϕ2)​(𝒫)→ψ⁡(𝒫)\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle_{(\phi_{1}\!\vee\!\phi_{2})(\mathcal{P})\to\psi(\mathcal{P})}, and δ1∨δ2\delta_{1}\!\vee\!\delta_{2} is the least common multiple of δ1\delta_{1} and δ2\delta_{2} in ⟨𝒞⟩𝒫→⋅\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle_{\mathcal{P}\to\cdot}. Similarly, for every morphism vv in 𝒫x→y\mathcal{P}_{x\to y} there exists a unique morphism ϕ1∧ϕ2​(v)\phi_{1}\!\wedge\!\phi_{2}(v) in 𝒞ϕ1∧ϕ2​(x)→ϕ1∧ϕ2​(y)\mathcal{C}_{\phi_{1}\!\wedge\!\phi_{2}(x)\to\phi_{1}\!\wedge\!\phi_{2}(y)} such that v​δ1∧δ2​(y)=δ1∧δ2​(x)​ϕ1∧ϕ2​(v)v\ \delta_{1}\!\wedge\!\delta_{2}\!(y)=\delta_{1}\!\wedge\!\delta_{2}\!(x)\ \phi_{1}\!\wedge\!\phi_{2}\!(v). Again, if 𝒞\mathcal{C} is a monoid the map ϕ1∧ϕ2\phi_{1}\!\wedge\!\phi_{2}\! is injective, and δ1∧δ2\delta_{1}\!\wedge\!\delta_{2} is the greatest common divisor of δ1\delta_{1} and δ2\delta_{2} in ⟨𝒞⟩𝒫→⋅\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle_{\mathcal{P}\to\cdot}. Thus, the set ⟨𝒞⟩𝒫→⋅\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle_{\mathcal{P}\to\cdot} is a lattice for the left-divisibility. By similar arguments, the set ⟨𝒞⟩⋅→𝒫\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle_{\cdot\to\mathcal{P}} is a lattice for the right-divisibility. ∎

As a direct consequence of Corollary 2.11 and Proposition 2.12, we get

Theorem 2.13.

Let (𝒞,Δ)(\mathcal{C},\Delta) be a monoidal Garside structure. Then, (⟨𝒞⟩,⟨Δ⟩)(\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle,\langle\Delta\rangle) is a categorical Garside structure.

Proof.

∎

2.5. The groupoid of subgroupoids

A subcategory that is a groupoid will be called a subgroupoid in the sequel. When (𝒞,Δ)(\mathcal{C},\Delta) is a categorical Garside structure such that ⟨𝒞⟩\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle is a Garside category, then 𝒢(⟨𝒞⟩)\mathcal{G}(\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle) is a Garside groupoid. There is another way to associate a groupoid with 𝒞\mathcal{C}. Indeed,

Definition 2.14 (Groupoid of subgroupoids).

Let 𝒢\mathcal{G} be a small groupoid. The groupoid of subgroupoids of 𝒢\mathcal{G} is the full subcategory 𝒩​⟨𝒢⟩\mathcal{N}\langle\mathcal{G}\rangle of the category ⟨𝒢⟩\langle\mathcal{G}\rangle whose objects are the subgroupoids of 𝒢\mathcal{G}.

Clearly, the category 𝒩​⟨𝒢⟩\mathcal{N}\langle\mathcal{G}\rangle is a groupoid. Then, 𝒩​⟨𝒢⁡(𝒞)⟩\mathcal{N}\langle\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{C})\rangle is a groupoid for every small category 𝒞\mathcal{C}. If GG is a group and PP is a subgroup, then 𝒩​⟨G⟩P→P\mathcal{N}\langle G\rangle_{P\to P} is the normalizer of PP in GG.

We recall that we denote by 𝒢⁡(F):𝒢⁡(𝒞)→𝒢⁡(𝒟)\mathcal{G}(F):\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{C})\to\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{D}) the functor induced by a functor F:𝒞→𝒟F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}.

Proposition 2.15.

Let 𝒞\mathcal{C} be a category. The canonical functor ι:𝒞→𝒢⁡(𝒞)\iota:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{C}) induces a functor ⟨ι⟩:⟨𝒞⟩→𝒩​⟨𝒢⁡(𝒞)⟩\langle\iota\rangle:\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle\to\mathop{\mathcal{N}\langle\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{C})\rangle}.

Proof.

For every object 𝒫\mathcal{P} of the category ⟨𝒞⟩\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle we set ⟨𝒫⟩=𝒢⁡(ι𝒫)​(𝒢⁡(𝒫))\langle\mathcal{P}\rangle=\mathcal{G}(\iota_{\mathcal{P}})(\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{P})). In other words, ⟨𝒫⟩\langle\mathcal{P}\rangle is the subgroupoid of 𝒢⁡(𝒞)\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{C}) generated by the subcategory ι⁡(𝒫)\iota(\mathcal{P}). Now, consider δ\delta in ⟨𝒞⟩𝒫→𝒬\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle_{\mathcal{P}\to\mathcal{Q}}, and denote by ϕ\phi its associated isomorphism. Let ⟨δ⟩\langle\delta\rangle be the map that sends an object xx of ⟨𝒫⟩\langle\mathcal{P}\rangle to the morphism ι⁡(δ⁡(x))\iota(\delta(x)). Then ⟨δ⟩\langle\delta\rangle belongs to 𝒩​⟨𝒢⁡(𝒞)⟩⟨𝒫⟩→⟨𝒬⟩\mathop{\mathcal{N}\langle\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{C})\rangle}_{\langle\mathcal{P}\rangle\to\langle\mathcal{Q}\rangle}. Indeed, Consider the map ⟨ϕ⟩:⟨𝒫⟩→⟨𝒬⟩\langle\phi\rangle:\langle\mathcal{P}\rangle\to\langle\mathcal{Q}\rangle which sends an object xx of ⟨𝒫⟩\langle\mathcal{P}\rangle to ϕ⁡(x)\phi(x) and a morphism vv in ⟨𝒫⟩x→y\langle\mathcal{P}\rangle_{x\to y} to (⟨δ⟩​(x))−1​v​⟨δ⟩​(y)(\langle\delta\rangle(x))^{-1}\,v\,\langle\delta\rangle(y). Then ⟨ϕ⟩\langle\phi\rangle is an isomorphism from ⟨𝒫⟩\langle\mathcal{P}\rangle to ⟨𝒬⟩\langle\mathcal{Q}\rangle and ⟨δ⟩\langle\delta\rangle is a natural transformation from ι⟨𝒫⟩\iota_{\langle\mathcal{P}\rangle} to ι⟨𝒬⟩∘⟨ϕ⟩\iota_{\langle\mathcal{Q}\rangle}\circ\langle\phi\rangle. Then we obtain a map ⟨ι⟩:⟨𝒞⟩→𝒩​⟨𝒢⁡(𝒞)⟩\langle\iota\rangle:\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle\to\mathop{\mathcal{N}\langle\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{C})\rangle} by setting ⟨ι⟩​(𝒫)=⟨𝒫⟩\langle\iota\rangle(\mathcal{P})=\langle\mathcal{P}\rangle and ⟨ι⟩​(δ)=⟨δ⟩\langle\iota\rangle(\delta)=\langle\delta\rangle. Clearly, this map is a functor. ∎

We remark that ⟨ι⟩\langle\iota\rangle is not injective in general: for two distinct subcategories 𝒫\mathcal{P} and 𝒬\mathcal{Q} we can have ⟨ι⟩​(𝒫)=⟨ι⟩​(𝒬)\langle\iota\rangle(\mathcal{P})=\langle\iota\rangle(\mathcal{Q}). For instance, consider the braid monoid B3+B^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{3} which is defined by the monoid presentation ⟨s,t∣sts=tst⟩\langle s,t\mid sts=tst\rangle; its group of fractions is the braid group B3B_{3}. The sets {s,t}\{s,t\} and {s,s​t​s}\{s,sts\} generate distinct submonoids of B3+B_{3}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}, but both generate the braid group B3B_{3}, as a group. Moreover, the functor ⟨ι⟩\langle\iota\rangle is neither faithful in general: the restriction of ⟨ι⟩\langle\iota\rangle to a set ⟨𝒞⟩𝒫→𝒬\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle_{\mathcal{P}\to\mathcal{Q}} is not always injective; if we consider the monoid MM defined by the monoid presentation ⟨a,b,c∣a2=a;ba=ac⟩\langle a,b,c\mid a^{2}=a\ ;\ ba=ac\rangle, and we denote by MbM_{b}, McM_{c} the submonoids generated by bb and cc, respectively, then aa is a non-trivial morphism in ⟨M⟩Mb→Mc\langle M\rangle_{M_{b}\to M_{c}}, whereas ι⁡(a)\iota(a) is trivial in 𝒢⁡(M)\mathcal{G}(M).

In the sequel, we write 𝒢⟨𝒞⟩\mathcal{G}\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle for 𝒢(⟨𝒞⟩)\mathcal{G}(\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle).

Proposition 2.16.

Let (𝒞,Δ)(\mathcal{C},\Delta) be a monoidal Garside structure. Denote by ι\iota the canonical embedding functor of 𝒞\mathcal{C} into 𝒢⁡(𝒞)\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{C}). The functor 𝒢⟨ι⟩:𝒢⟨𝒞⟩→𝒩​⟨𝒢⁡(𝒞)⟩\mathcal{G}\!\langle\iota\rangle:\mathcal{G}\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle\to\mathop{\mathcal{N}\langle\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{C})\rangle} is faithful.

Proof.

Let 𝒫\mathcal{P} and 𝒬\mathcal{Q} be two objects of 𝒢⟨𝒞⟩\mathcal{G}\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle and consider δ\delta, τ\tau in 𝒢⟨𝒞⟩𝒫→𝒬\mathcal{G}\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle_{\mathcal{P}\to\mathcal{Q}} such that 𝒢​⟨ι⟩​(δ)=𝒢​⟨ι⟩​(τ)\mathcal{G}\!\langle\iota\rangle(\delta)=\mathcal{G}\!\langle\iota\rangle(\tau). Then, 𝒢​⟨ι⟩​(τ−1​δ)=1𝒢⁡(𝒫)\mathcal{G}\!\langle\iota\rangle(\tau^{-1}\delta)=1_{\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{P})}. Then, it is enough to assume for the rest of the proof that 𝒫=𝒬\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{Q}~ and τ=1𝒫\tau=1_{\mathcal{P}}. Since the category ⟨𝒞⟩\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle is a Garside category, we can identify ⟨𝒞⟩\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle with its image in its group of fractions 𝒢⟨𝒞⟩\mathcal{G}\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle, and decompose the morphism δ\delta as a product δ1​δ2−1\delta_{1}\delta_{2}^{-1} with δ1\delta_{1} and δ2\delta_{2} in ⟨𝒞⟩𝒫→𝒫′\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle_{\mathcal{P}\to\mathcal{P}^{\prime}} for some object 𝒫′\mathcal{P}^{\prime} of ⟨𝒞⟩\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle. Since 𝒢​⟨ι⟩​(δ)=1𝒢⁡(𝒫)\mathcal{G}\!\langle\iota\rangle(\delta)=1_{\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{P})}, we have 𝒢​⟨ι⟩​(δ1)=𝒢​⟨ι⟩​(δ2)\mathcal{G}\!\langle\iota\rangle(\delta_{1})=\mathcal{G}\!\langle\iota\rangle(\delta_{2}), that is, ⟨ι⟩​(δ1)=⟨ι⟩​(δ2)\langle\iota\rangle(\delta_{1})=\langle\iota\rangle(\delta_{2}). By definition, this means that for every object xx of 𝒫\mathcal{P}, we have ι⁡(δ1​(x))=ι⁡(δ2​(x))\iota(\delta_{1}(x))=\iota(\delta_{2}(x)). But ι\iota is an injective functor. Then δ1=δ2\delta_{1}=\delta_{2} and δ=1𝒫\delta=1_{\mathcal{P}}. ∎

As a final comment to this section, we remark that the morphism ⟨ι⟩\langle\iota\rangle is not injective on the objects. Therefore, the groupoid 𝒢⟨𝒞⟩\mathcal{G}\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle cannot be seen as a subgroupoid of 𝒩​⟨𝒢⁡(𝒞)⟩\mathcal{N}\langle\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{C})\rangle.

3. The ribbon groupoid

In this section, we introduce and investigate the positive ribbon category and the ribbon groupoid. This ribbon category is defined as a full subcategory of the category ⟨𝒞⟩\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle. The ribbon groupoid is defined as a full subgroupoid of 𝒩​⟨𝒢⁡(𝒞)⟩\mathcal{N}\langle\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{C})\rangle, which turns out to be, under some restriction, the group of fractions of the positive ribbon category. We first define the notion of a parabolic subgroupoid.

3.1. Parabolic subgroupoids

Here we extend the notion of a parabolic subgroup of a Garside group [17] into the framework of Garside groupoids. If 𝒞\mathcal{C} is a category and δ\delta lies in 𝒞x→⋅\mathcal{C}_{x\to\cdot}, then we denote by [1x,δ]𝒞[1_{x},\delta]_{\mathcal{C}} the set of elements between 1x1_{x} and δ\delta for the left-divisibility in 𝒞x→⋅\mathcal{C}_{x\to\cdot}.

Definition 3.1 (Parabolic subcategories).

Let (𝒞,Δ)(\mathcal{C},\Delta) be a categorical Garside structure. A subcategory 𝒫\mathcal{P} of 𝒞\mathcal{C} is a parabolic subcategory of 𝒞\mathcal{C} if for every object xx of 𝒫\mathcal{P} the sets 𝒫x→⋅\mathcal{P}_{x\to\cdot} and 𝒫⋅→x\mathcal{P}_{\cdot\to x} are sublattices of 𝒞x→⋅\mathcal{C}_{x\to\cdot} and 𝒞⋅→x\mathcal{C}_{\cdot\to x}, respectively, and, there exists δ\delta in ⟨𝒞⟩𝒫→𝒫\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle_{\mathcal{P}\to\mathcal{P}} such that for every object xx of 𝒫\mathcal{P}, one has

[1x,δ(x)]𝒞=[1x,Δ(x)]𝒞∩𝒫x→⋅=Δ(x)∧𝒫x→⋅[1_{x},\delta(x)]_{\mathcal{C}}=[1_{x},\Delta(x)]_{\mathcal{C}}\cap\mathcal{P}_{x\to\cdot}=\Delta(x)\wedge\mathcal{P}_{x\to\cdot}

in the lattice 𝒞x→⋅\mathcal{C}_{x\to\cdot}.

With the notation of the above definition, when 𝒫\mathcal{P} is a parabolic subcategory then one has [1x,Δ(x)]𝒞∩𝒫x→⋅=[1x,δ(x)]𝒫[1_{x},\Delta(x)]_{\mathcal{C}}\cap\mathcal{P}_{x\to\cdot}=[1_{x},\delta(x)]_{\mathcal{P}}, and the atoms of 𝒫\mathcal{P} are the atoms of 𝒞\mathcal{C} that lie in 𝒫\mathcal{P}. It is immediate that the pair (𝒫,δ)(\mathcal{P},\delta) is a categorical Garside structure. Furthermore, the canonical embedding functor from 𝒫\mathcal{P} to 𝒞\mathcal{C} induces an injective functor from 𝒢⁡(𝒫)\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{P}) to 𝒢⁡(𝒞)\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{C}) such that the following diagram is commutative:

𝒫↪𝒞↓↓𝒢⁡(𝒫)↪𝒢⁡(𝒞)\begin{array}[]{ccc}\mathcal{P}&\hookrightarrow&\mathcal{C}\\ \downarrow&&\downarrow\\ \mathcal{G}(\mathcal{P})&\hookrightarrow&\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{C})\end{array}

Therefore, we can identify 𝒢⁡(𝒫)\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{P}) with a subgroupoid of 𝒢⁡(𝒞)\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{C}). In that context, we have 𝒫=𝒢⁡(𝒫)∩𝒞\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{P})\cap\mathcal{C} (where the notion of an intersection of two subcategories is defined in an obvious way).

Definition 3.2 (Parabolic subgroupoids).

Let (𝒞,Δ)(\mathcal{C},\Delta) be a categorical Garside structure.
A subgroupoid of the Garside groupoid 𝒢⁡(𝒞)\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{C}) is a standard parabolic subgroupoid when it is the groupoid of formal inverses 𝒢⁡(𝒫)\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{P}) of a parabolic subcategory 𝒫\mathcal{P} of 𝒞\mathcal{C}. A non empty subgroupoid 𝒢\mathcal{G} of 𝒢⁡(𝒞)\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{C}) is a parabolic subgroupoid if there exists a standard parabolic subgroupoid 𝒢⁡(𝒫)\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{P}) such that 𝒩​⟨𝒢⁡(𝒞)⟩𝒢⁡(𝒫)→𝒢\mathop{\mathcal{N}\langle\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{C})\rangle}_{\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{P})\to\mathcal{G}} is not empty.

Example 3.3.

In the context of Garside groups, we recover the notion of a standard parabolic subgroup introduced in [17], which extends the notion of a standard parabolic subgroup of an Artin-Tits group. Standard parabolic subgroups of an Artin-Tits group AA are the subgroups generated by any set of atoms of the associated Artin-Tits monoid A+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+} (cf. Example 2.3)). In the sequel, we denote by AIA_{I} the standard parabolic subgroup of a Garside group AA generated by a set II of atoms of A+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}.

We only consider parabolic subgroupoids that are standard in the sequel. Therefore, we write parabolic for standard parabolic in the sequel.

Example 3.4.

Consider the free group F2F_{2} on two letters a,ba,b and the Garside structure of Example 2.4. In this context, Except the whole group F2F_{2} and the trivial subgroup, a parabolic subgroup of F2F_{2} is any subgroup generated by one generator aia_{i}. Then, parabolic proper subgroups are all isomorphic to ℤ\mathbb{Z}.

Example 3.5.

Direct product of Garside groups are Garside groups. For instance, the group AA defined by the group presentation ⟨a,b,c∣a2=b2,ac=ca,bc=cb⟩\langle a,b,c\mid a^{2}=b^{2},ac=ca,bc=cb\rangle is a Garside group, with a2​ca^{2}c as Garside element. Its parabolic subgroups are the four subgroups {1}\{1\}, A{a,b}A_{\{a,b\}}, A{c}A_{\{c\}} and AA.

Example 3.6.

The group AA defined by the presentation ⟨a,b,c∣aba=bab=c2⟩\langle a,b,c\mid aba=bab=c^{2}\rangle is a Garside group, with a​b​aaba as Garside element. Indeed, amalgam products of Garside groups above their Garside elements are Garside groups. The parabolic subgroups of AA are the four subgroups ∅\emptyset, A{a}A_{\{a\}}, A{b}A_{\{b\}} and AA.

It is quite easy to see that most of the properties proved in [17] can be extended into the context of Garside groupoid, with similar proof.

3.2. Positive ribbon category

We are now ready to define the ribbon groupoid, whose objects are the parabolic subgroupoids.

Definition 3.7 (Positive ribbon category).

Let (𝒞​Δ)(\mathcal{C}\Delta) be a categorical Garside structure. The positive ribbon category ℛ+​(𝒞)\mathop{\mathcal{R^{\scriptscriptstyle+}}\!(\mathcal{C})} associated with 𝒞\mathcal{C} is the full subcategory of ⟨𝒞⟩\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle whose objects are the parabolic subcategories of 𝒞\mathcal{C}.

We recall that for every parabolic subcategory 𝒫\mathcal{P} of 𝒞\mathcal{C}, we have identified 𝒢⁡(𝒫)\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{P}) with a subgroupoid of 𝒢⁡(𝒞)\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{C}). We also recall that 𝒫=𝒞∩𝒢⁡(𝒫)\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{C}\cap\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{P}) and that the categories 𝒫\mathcal{P} and 𝒢⁡(𝒫)\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{P}) have the same objects. In particular every element δ\delta of ⟨𝒢⁡(𝒞)⟩𝒢⁡(𝒫)→𝒢⁡(𝒬)\langle\mathop{\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{C})}\rangle_{\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{P})\to\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{Q})} belongs to ⟨𝒢⁡(𝒞)⟩𝒫→ϕ⁡(𝒫)\langle\mathop{\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{C})}\rangle_{\mathcal{P}\to\phi(\mathcal{P})}, where ϕ\phi is the isomorphism associated with δ\delta.

Definition 3.8 (Ribbon groupoid).

Let (𝒞,Δ)(\mathcal{C},\Delta) be a categorical Garside structure.
(i) If 𝒢⁡(𝒫)\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{P}) and 𝒢⁡(𝒬)\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{Q}) are two parabolic subgroupoids, then a ribbon from the former to the latter is a morphism δ\delta in ⟨𝒢⁡(𝒞)⟩𝒢⁡(𝒫)→𝒢⁡(𝒬)\langle\mathop{\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{C})}\rangle_{\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{P})\to\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{Q})} that belongs to ⟨𝒢⁡(𝒞)⟩𝒫→𝒬\langle\mathop{\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{C})}\rangle_{\mathcal{P}\to\mathcal{Q}}.
(ii) The ribbon groupoid ℛ⁡(𝒞)\mathop{\mathcal{R}\!(\mathcal{C})} of 𝒢⁡(𝒞)\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{C}) is the subcategory of 𝒩​⟨𝒢⁡(𝒞)⟩\mathop{\mathcal{N}\langle\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{C})\rangle} whose objects are the standard parabolic subgroupoids of 𝒢⁡(𝒞)\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{C}) and whose morphisms are the ribbons.

Example 3.9.

Consider the free group F2F_{2} on two letters a,ba,b, and the Garside structure of Examples 2.4 and 3.4. Then, each object of the groupoid ℛ⁡(F2)\mathcal{R}(F_{2}) distinct from the trivial subgroup and the whole group can be identified with one of the aia_{i}. Clearly, there are morphisms between aia_{i} and aja_{j} in ℛ⁡(F2)\mathcal{R}(F_{2}) if and only if i−ji-j is even.

The category ℛ⁡(𝒞)\mathop{\mathcal{R}\!(\mathcal{C})} is clearly a groupoid and the image by ⟨ι⟩\langle\iota\rangle of a morphism of ℛ+​(𝒞)\mathop{\mathcal{R^{\scriptscriptstyle+}}\!(\mathcal{C})} is a ribbon. In the sequel such a ribbon is called a positive ribbon. Indeed,

Proposition 3.10.

Let (𝒞,Δ)(\mathcal{C},\Delta) be a categorical Garside structure such that the vertex set of 𝒞\mathcal{C} is finite. Denote by Φ\Phi the automorphism of 𝒞\mathcal{C} induced by Δ\Delta.
(i) The category ℛ+​(𝒞)\mathop{\mathcal{R^{\scriptscriptstyle+}}\!(\mathcal{C})} is cancellative and noetherian.
(ii) The functor ⟨Φ⟩\langle\Phi\rangle restricts to an automorphism ⟨Φ⟩\langle\Phi\rangle of ℛ+​(𝒞)\mathop{\mathcal{R^{\scriptscriptstyle+}}\!(\mathcal{C})}. The restriction of ⟨Δ⟩\langle\Delta\rangle to the vertex set of ℛ+​(𝒞)\mathop{\mathcal{R^{\scriptscriptstyle+}}\!(\mathcal{C})} is a natural transformation from the identity functor of ℛ+​(𝒞)\mathop{\mathcal{R^{\scriptscriptstyle+}}\!(\mathcal{C})} to this restricted automorphism.
(iii) When 𝒞\mathcal{C} is a monoid, the functor ⟨ι⟩:⟨𝒞⟩→𝒩​⟨𝒢⁡(𝒞)⟩\langle\iota\rangle:\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle\to\mathop{\mathcal{N}\langle\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{C})\rangle} is injective on to the category ℛ+​(𝒞)\mathop{\mathcal{R^{\scriptscriptstyle+}}\!(\mathcal{C})} and the image ⟨ι⟩​(ℛ+​(𝒞))\langle\iota\rangle(\mathop{\mathcal{R^{\scriptscriptstyle+}}\!(\mathcal{C})}) is a subcategory of ℛ⁡(𝒞)\mathop{\mathcal{R}\!(\mathcal{C})}. Moreover the morphism 𝒢​⟨ι⟩\mathcal{G}\!\langle\iota\rangle induces an isomorphism of groupoids from 𝒢⁡(ℛ+​(𝒞))\mathcal{G}(\mathop{\mathcal{R^{\scriptscriptstyle+}}\!(\mathcal{C})}) to ℛ⁡(𝒞)\mathop{\mathcal{R}\!(\mathcal{C})}.

Proof.

(i)(i) ℛ+​(𝒞)\mathop{\mathcal{R^{\scriptscriptstyle+}}\!(\mathcal{C})} is cancellative and noetherian since it is a subcategory of ⟨𝒞⟩\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle.
(i​i)(ii) From the equality Φ⁡(Δ⁡(x))=Δ⁡(Φ⁡(x))\Phi(\Delta(x))=\Delta(\Phi(x)) and the definition of a parabolic subcategory, it follows that Φ⁡(𝒫)\Phi(\mathcal{P}) is a parabolic subcategory if and only if 𝒫\mathcal{P} is a parabolic subcategory. Moreover, in this case the map ⟨Δ⟩​(𝒫)\langle\Delta\rangle(\mathcal{P}) lies in ℛ+​(𝒞)𝒫→Φ⁡(𝒫)\mathop{\mathcal{R^{\scriptscriptstyle+}}\!(\mathcal{C})}_{\mathcal{P}\to\Phi(\mathcal{P})}.
(i​i​i)(iii) By construction, the image of ℛ+​(𝒞)\mathop{\mathcal{R^{\scriptscriptstyle+}}\!(\mathcal{C})} by ⟨ι⟩\langle\iota\rangle is a subcategory of ℛ⁡(𝒞)\mathop{\mathcal{R}\!(\mathcal{C})}. Furthermore, we already know that ⟨ι⟩\langle\iota\rangle is faithful by Proposition 2.16. Now, if 𝒫1\mathcal{P}_{1}, 𝒫2\mathcal{P}_{2} are two objects of ℛ+​(𝒞)\mathop{\mathcal{R^{\scriptscriptstyle+}}\!(\mathcal{C})}, then one has

𝒫1=𝒞∩𝒢⁡(𝒫1)=𝒞∩⟨ι⟩​(𝒫1)=𝒞∩⟨ι⟩​(𝒫2)=𝒞∩𝒢⁡(𝒫2)=𝒫2\mathcal{P}_{1}=\mathcal{C}\cap\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{P}_{1})=\mathcal{C}\cap\langle\iota\rangle(\mathcal{P}_{1})=\mathcal{C}\cap\langle\iota\rangle(\mathcal{P}_{2})=\mathcal{C}\cap\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{P}_{2})=\mathcal{P}_{2}

Hence, ⟨ι⟩\langle\iota\rangle lies injective on ℛ+​(𝒞)\mathop{\mathcal{R^{\scriptscriptstyle+}}\!(\mathcal{C})}. Using that ⟨𝒞⟩\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle is a Garside category, we get that 𝒢​⟨ι⟩\mathcal{G}\!\langle\iota\rangle induces an isomorphism of groupoids from the subgroupoid  𝒢⁡(ℛ+​(𝒞))\mathcal{G}(\mathop{\mathcal{R^{\scriptscriptstyle+}}\!(\mathcal{C})}) to its image, which lies in ℛ⁡(𝒞)\mathop{\mathcal{R}\!(\mathcal{C})}. Let δ\delta lie in ℛ⁡(𝒞)𝒢⁡(𝒫)→𝒢⁡(𝒬)\mathop{\mathcal{R}\!(\mathcal{C})}_{\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{P})\to\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{Q})} and ϕ:𝒢⁡(𝒫)→𝒢⁡(𝒬)\phi:\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{P})\to\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{Q}) be its associated isomorphism. We can decompose δ\delta as a product δ=δ1​Δ−n\delta=\delta_{1}\Delta^{-n} for some non negative integer nn and some δ1\delta_{1} in the monoid 𝒞\mathcal{C}. Now, the element δ1\delta_{1} belongs to ℛ+​(𝒞)𝒫→Φn​(𝒬)\mathop{\mathcal{R^{\scriptscriptstyle+}}\!(\mathcal{C})}_{\mathcal{P}\to\Phi^{n}(\mathcal{Q})} since (Φn∘ϕ)​(𝒫)=Φn​(Q)(\Phi^{n}\circ\phi)(\mathcal{P})=\Phi^{n}(Q). Therefore, the image of 𝒢⁡(ℛ+​(𝒞))\mathcal{G}(\mathop{\mathcal{R^{\scriptscriptstyle+}}\!(\mathcal{C})}) by ⟨ι⟩\langle\iota\rangle is ℛ⁡(𝒞)\mathop{\mathcal{R}\!(\mathcal{C})}. ∎

As a consequence of the previous result, we get

Proposition 3.11.

Let (𝒞,Δ)(\mathcal{C},\Delta) be a categorical Garside structure such that 𝒞\mathcal{C} is a monoid. Assume the sets ℛ+​(𝒞)𝒫→⋅\mathop{\mathcal{R^{\scriptscriptstyle+}}\!(\mathcal{C})}_{\mathcal{P}\to\cdot} and ℛ+​(𝒞)⋅→𝒫\mathop{\mathcal{R^{\scriptscriptstyle+}}\!(\mathcal{C})}_{\cdot\to\mathcal{P}} are sublattices of ⟨𝒞⟩𝒫→⋅\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle_{\mathcal{P}\to\cdot} and ⟨𝒞⟩⋅→𝒫\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle_{\cdot\to\mathcal{P}}, respectively, for every parabolic submonoid 𝒫\mathcal{P} of 𝒞\mathcal{C}. Then (ℛ+​(𝒞),⟨Δ⟩)(\mathop{\mathcal{R^{\scriptscriptstyle+}}\!(\mathcal{C})},\langle\Delta\rangle) is a categorical Garside structure with ℛ⁡(𝒞)\mathop{\mathcal{R}\!(\mathcal{C})} as associated Garside groupoid.

Proof.

∎

Generalizing the terminology of [17] to Garside groupoids, we could say under the assumption of Proposition 3.11 that ℛ+​(𝒞)\mathop{\mathcal{R^{\scriptscriptstyle+}}\!(\mathcal{C})} is a Garside subcategory of ⟨𝒞⟩\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle.

3.3. Garside groups with a ν\nu-structure

In the previous sections, we prove, under some technical assumptions, that the category of subcategories of a Garside ⟨𝒞⟩\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle category 𝒞\mathcal{C} is itself a Garside category. In particular this is always the case when 𝒞\mathcal{C} is a Garside monoid. We prove that, moreover, the positive ribbon category ℛ+​(𝒞)\mathop{\mathcal{R^{\scriptscriptstyle+}}\!(\mathcal{C})} is also a Garside category, with the ribbon groupoid ℛ⁡(𝒞)\mathop{\mathcal{R}\!(\mathcal{C})} as associated Garside groupoid, under the assumption that this positive ribbon category ℛ+​(𝒞)\mathop{\mathcal{R^{\scriptscriptstyle+}}\!(\mathcal{C})} respects the lattice structure of the category of subcategories ⟨𝒞⟩\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle. In this section, we consider a simple criteria which insures that ℛ+​(𝒞)\mathop{\mathcal{R^{\scriptscriptstyle+}}\!(\mathcal{C})} respects the lattice structure of ⟨𝒞⟩\langle\mathop{\mathcal{C}}\rangle. The criteria is verified by Artin-Tits groups of spherical type.

We recall that a monoidal Garside structure (A+,Δ)(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+},\Delta) is a categorical Garside structure such that A+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+} is a monoid; we denote by AA the associated Garside group. We denote by AX+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{X} a parabolic submonoid of A+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+} whose atom set is XX. We denote by AXA_{X} the associated standard parabolic subgroup. We recall that, in this context, an element gg of ℛ+​(A+)AX+→AY+\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}_{A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\to A_{Y}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}} is an element of A+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+} such that g−1​AX+​g=AY+g^{-1}A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{X}g=A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{Y} (which is equivalent to g−1​X​g=Yg^{-1}Xg=Y).

From now on, for g,hg,h in (A+CLOSE(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}, we denote by g∨hg\lor h and g∧hg\land h their lcm and their gcd for the left-divisibility, respectively, and we denote by g​∨~​hg\tilde{\lor}h and g​∧~​hg\tilde{\land}h their lcm and their gcd for the right-divisibility, respectively.

Definition 3.12 (ν\nu-structure).

Let (A+,Δ)(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+},\Delta) be a monoidal Garside structure. Let SS be the atom set of A+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}.
(i) We say that A+A^{+} has a ν\nu-function if for each parabolic submonoid AX+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{X} there exists a map νX:S→ℛ+(A+)AX+→⋅\nu_{X}:S\to\mathcal{R^{\scriptscriptstyle+}}(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})_{A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\to\cdot} such that

  1. (1)

    for every ss in SS, the morphism νX​(s)\nu_{X}(s) is an atom of ℛ+​(A+)\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})};

  2. (2)

    for every ss in SS and every gg in ℛ+​(A+)AX+→⋅\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}_{A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\to\cdot}, if ss left-divides gg then νX​(s)\nu_{X}(s) left-divides gg;

  3. (3)

    for every s,ts,t in SS, the lcm of νX​(s)\nu_{X}(s) and νX​(t)\nu_{X}(t) for left-divisibility lies in ℛ+​(A+)AX+→⋅\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}_{A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\to\cdot}.

(ii) We say that A+A^{+} has a ν~\tilde{\nu}-function if for each parabolic submonoid AX+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{X} there exists a map ν~X:S→ℛ+​(A+)⋅→AX+\tilde{\nu}_{X}:S\to\mathcal{R^{\scriptscriptstyle+}}(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})_{\cdot\to A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}} such that

  1. (1)

    for every ss in SS, the morphism ν~X​(s)\tilde{\nu}_{X}(s) is an atom of ℛ+​(A+)\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})};

  2. (2)

    for every ss in SS and every gg in ℛ+​(A+)⋅→AX+\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}_{\cdot\to A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}}, if ss right-divides gg then ν~X​(s)\tilde{\nu}_{X}(s) right-divides gg;

  3. (3)

    for every s,ts,t in SS, the lcm of ν~X​(s)\tilde{\nu}_{X}(s) and ν~X​(t)\tilde{\nu}_{X}(t) for right-divisibility lies in ℛ+​(A+)⋅→AX+\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}_{\cdot\to A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}}.

(iii) We say that A+A^{+} has a ν\nu-structure if it has both a ν\nu-function and a ν~\tilde{\nu}-function.

Remark 3.13.

(i) We do not require that ss left-divides νX​(s)\nu_{X}(s).
(ii) When AA has a ν\nu-function (resp. a ν~\tilde{\nu}-function), then each atom of ℛ+​(A+)\mathcal{R^{\scriptscriptstyle+}}(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}) that belongs to ℛ+(A+)AX+→⋅\mathcal{R^{\scriptscriptstyle+}}(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})_{A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\to\cdot} (resp. to ℛ+​(A+)⋅→AX+\mathcal{R^{\scriptscriptstyle+}}(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})_{\cdot\to A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}}) is equal to some νX​(s)\nu_{X}(s) (resp. some ν~X​(s)\tilde{\nu}_{X}(s)). Furthermore, if gg is an atom of ℛ+​(A+)\mathcal{R^{\scriptscriptstyle+}}(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}) that belongs to ℛ+(A+)AX+→⋅\mathcal{R^{\scriptscriptstyle+}}(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})_{A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\to\cdot} (resp. to ℛ+​(A+)⋅→AX+\mathcal{R^{\scriptscriptstyle+}}(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})_{\cdot\to A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}}) and ss in SS left-divides (resp. right-divides) gg, then g=νX​(s)g=\nu_{X}(s) (resp. g=ν~X​(s)g=\tilde{\nu}_{X}(s)).

Example 3.14.

Every Artin-Tits monoid of spherical type (cf. Example 3.5) has a ν\nu-structure. Consider the notation of Example 3.5. Let XX be a subset of SS and ss lie in SS. If ss does not belong to XX, we set νX​(s)=ΔX−1​ΔX∪{s}\nu_{X}(s)=\Delta_{X}^{-1}\Delta_{X\cup\{s\}} and ν~X​(s)=ΔX∪{s}​ΔX−1\tilde{\nu}_{X}(s)=\Delta_{X\cup\{s\}}\Delta_{X}^{-1}; if ss lies in XX, we set νX​(s)=ν~X​(s)=ΔXi\nu_{X}(s)=\tilde{\nu}_{X}(s)=\Delta_{X_{i}} where XiX_{i} is the indecomposable component of XX that contains ss. We recall that an Artin-Tits group of spherical type is said to be indecomposable when it is not the direct product of two of its proper standard parabolic subgroups. It follows from [15] that these functions provide a ν\nu-structure to the Artin-Tits monoid.

Proposition 3.15.

Let (A+,Δ)(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+},\Delta) be a monoidal Garside structure.
(i) If AA has a ν\nu-function, then the set ℛ+(A+)AX+→⋅\mathcal{R^{\scriptscriptstyle+}}(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})_{A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\to\cdot} is a sublattice of ⟨𝐴+⟩AX+→⋅\langle\mathop{A}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\rangle_{A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\to\cdot} for every parabolic submonoid AX+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{X}.
(ii) If AA has a ν~\tilde{\nu}-function then the set ℛ+​(A+)⋅→AX+\mathcal{R^{\scriptscriptstyle+}}(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})_{\cdot\to A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}} is a sublattice of ⟨𝐴+⟩⋅→AX+\langle\mathop{A}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\rangle_{\cdot\to A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}} for every parabolic submonoid AX+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{X}.

gcd’s: By the second defining property of a ν\nu-function, if ss left-divides both gg and hh then νX​(s)\nu_{X}(s) left-divides both gg and hh.
