From Propositions 3.11 and 3.15 we obtain Theorem 1.1, which applies in the case of Artin-Tits groups of spherical type. The latter groups are not the only Garside groups which have a ν\nu-structure:

Corollary 3.16.

(i) Consider the notation of Example 2.4. The category ℛ+​(F2+)\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(F_{2}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}) is a Garside category with ℛ⁡(F2)\mathcal{R}\!(F_{2}) as associated Garside groupoid.
(ii) The category ℛ+​(A+)\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})} of the Garside group AA of Example 3.5 is a Garside category with ℛ⁡(A)\mathop{\mathcal{R}\!(A)} as associated Garside groupoid.
(iii) The category ℛ+​(A+)\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})} of the Garside group AA of Example 3.6 is a Garside category with ℛ⁡(A)\mathop{\mathcal{R}\!(A)} as associated Garside groupoid.

Proof.

We only need to explicit a ν\nu-structure in each case:
 (i)(i) for X=∅X=\emptyset and i∈ℤi\in\mathbb{Z}, one has νX​(ai)=ν~X​(ai)=ai\nu_{X}(a_{i})=\tilde{\nu}_{X}(a_{i})=a_{i}; for X={aj∣j∈ℤ}X=\{a_{j}\mid j\in\mathbb{Z}\} and i∈ℤi\in\mathbb{Z}, one has νX​(ai)=ν~X​(ai)=a0​a1\nu_{X}(a_{i})=\tilde{\nu}_{X}(a_{i})=a_{0}a_{1}; for X={aj}X=\{a_{j}\} and i∈ℤi\in\mathbb{Z} with i≠ji\neq j, one has νX​(aj)=ν~X​(aj)=aj\nu_{X}(a_{j})=\tilde{\nu}_{X}(a_{j})=a_{j}, νX​(ai)=aj+1\nu_{X}(a_{i})=a_{j+1}, and ν~X​(ai)=aj−1\tilde{\nu}_{X}(a_{i})=a_{j-1}.
(i​i)(ii) for X=∅X=\emptyset or X={c}X=\{c\} and t=a,b,ct=a,b,c, one has νX​(t)=ν~X​(t)=t\nu_{X}(t)=\tilde{\nu}_{X}(t)=t; for X={a,b,c}X=\{a,b,c\} and t=a,b,ct=a,b,c, one has νX​(t)=ν~X​(t)=a2​c\nu_{X}(t)=\tilde{\nu}_{X}(t)=a^{2}c; for X={a,b}X=\{a,b\}, one has νX​(a)=ν~X​(a)=νX​(b)=ν~X​(b)=a2\nu_{X}(a)=\tilde{\nu}_{X}(a)=\nu_{X}(b)=\tilde{\nu}_{X}(b)=a^{2}, and νX​(c)=ν~X​(c)=c\nu_{X}(c)=\tilde{\nu}_{X}(c)=c.
(i​i​i)(iii) for X=∅X=\emptyset and t=a,b,ct=a,b,c, one has νX​(t)=ν~X​(t)=t\nu_{X}(t)=\tilde{\nu}_{X}(t)=t; for X={a,b,c}X=\{a,b,c\} and t=a,b,ct=a,b,c, one has νX​(t)=ν~X​(t)=c2\nu_{X}(t)=\tilde{\nu}_{X}(t)=c^{2}; for X={a}X=\{a\}, one has νX​(a)=ν~X​(a)=a\nu_{X}(a)=\tilde{\nu}_{X}(a)=a, νX​(b)=νX​(c)=b​a\nu_{X}(b)=\nu_{X}(c)=ba and ν~X​(b)=ν~X​(c)=a​b\tilde{\nu}_{X}(b)=\tilde{\nu}_{X}(c)=ab; for X={b}X=\{b\}, one has νX​(b)=ν~−X⁡(b)=b\nu_{X}(b)=\tilde{\nu}-X(b)=b, νX​(a)=νX​(c)=a​b\nu_{X}(a)=\nu_{X}(c)=ab and ν~X​(a)=ν~X​(c)=b​a\tilde{\nu}_{X}(a)=\tilde{\nu}_{X}(c)=ba. ∎

4. Presentation of groupoids

Given a group, it is a classical question to obtain a presentation of this group. Here, we consider the similar problem in the context of groupoids. For all this section we fix a monoidal Garside structure (OPENA+,Δ)A^{\scriptscriptstyle+},\Delta), such that the Garside monoid A+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+} has a ν\nu-structure. We denote by SS the atom set of A+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+} and by AA its group of fractions. In the previous section, we have seen that the ribbon groupoid ℛ⁡(A)\mathop{\mathcal{R}\!(A)} is a Garside groupoid. Let us first precise the notion of a groupoid presentation. We recall that the free category 𝒞⁡(Γ)\mathcal{C}(\Gamma) associated with a graph Γ\Gamma has been defined in Section 2.1.

Definition 4.1 (Generating quiver).

Let 𝒞\mathcal{C} be a small category. Let Γ\Gamma be a quiver whose vertex set is the object set of 𝒞\mathcal{C} and whose edges are morphisms of 𝒞\mathcal{C}.
(i) We say that Γ\Gamma generates 𝒞\mathcal{C} as a category if the canonical map from Γ\Gamma to 𝒞\mathcal{C} extends to a surjective functor from the free category 𝒞⁡(Γ)\mathcal{C}(\Gamma) to the category 𝒞\mathcal{C}.
(ii) If 𝒞\mathcal{C} is a groupoid, we say that Γ\Gamma generates 𝒞\mathcal{C} as a groupoid if the canonical map from Γ\Gamma to 𝒞\mathcal{C} extends to a surjective functor from the free groupoid 𝒢⁡(𝒞⁡(Γ))\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{C}(\Gamma)) to the groupoid 𝒞\mathcal{C}.

Definition 4.2 (Groupoid presentation).

Let 𝒞\mathcal{C} be a small category. Consider a quiver Γ\Gamma and a set R={(gi,hi),i∈I}R=\{(g_{i},h_{i}),i\in I\} of morphisms of 𝒞⁡(Γ)\mathcal{C}(\Gamma) with the same source and the same target. Denote by ≡R\equiv_{R} is the congruence on ℳ⁡(Γ)\mathcal{M}(\Gamma) generated by RR.
(i) We say that ⟨Γ,R⟩\langle\Gamma,R\rangle is a presentation of 𝒞\mathcal{C} as a category if Γ\Gamma generates 𝒞\mathcal{C} as a category and the surjective functor from 𝒞⁡(Γ)\mathcal{C}(\Gamma) to 𝒞\mathcal{C} induces an isomorphism of categories from 𝒞(Γ,≡R)\mathcal{C}(\Gamma,\equiv_{R}) to 𝒞\mathcal{C}.
(ii) When 𝒞\mathcal{C} is a groupoid, we say that ⟨Γ,R⟩\langle\Gamma,R\rangle is a presentation of 𝒞\mathcal{C} as a groupoid if Γ\Gamma generates 𝒞\mathcal{C} as a groupoid and the surjective functor from 𝒢⁡(𝒞⁡(Γ))\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{C}(\Gamma)) to 𝒞\mathcal{C} induces an isomorphism of groupoid from 𝒢(𝒞(Γ,≡R))\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{C}(\Gamma,\equiv_{R})) to 𝒞\mathcal{C}.

In the sequel, we write gi=hig_{i}=h_{i} for (gi,hi)(g_{i},h_{i}) in the category/groupoid presentations. Our main objective in this section is to obtain a groupoid presentation of the groupoid of ℛ⁡(A)\mathop{\mathcal{R}\!(A)}.

Lemma 4.3.

Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be the graph whose vertices are the standard parabolic subgroups of AA, and whose edge set is the image of the ν\nu-functions: to each element νX​(s)\nu_{X}(s) that lies in ℛ+​(A+)AX→AY\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}_{A_{X}\to A_{Y}} corresponds an edge from AXA_{X} to AYA_{Y} in 𝒜\mathcal{A}. The quiver 𝒜\mathcal{A} generates ℛ+​(A+)\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})} as a category and ℛ⁡(A)\mathop{\mathcal{R}\!(A)} as a groupoid.

The reader should remember that for s≠ts\neq t we can have νX​(s)=νX​(t)\nu_{X}(s)=\nu_{X}(t); in that case, the pairs (X,s)(X,s) and (X,t)(X,t) correspond to the same edge in the quiver 𝒜\mathcal{A}.

Proof.

The atom graph of ℛ+​(A+)\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})} is a generating quiver and the image of the ν\nu-functions is precisely the atom set of the category ℛ+​(A+)\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})} (see Section 2.3). Furthermore, ℛ⁡(A)\mathop{\mathcal{R}\!(A)} is the group of fractions of the Garside category ℛ+​(A+)\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}. ∎

In the case of an Artin-Tits group of spherical type, we have seen in Example 3.14 that there is two types of atoms in ℛ⁡(A)\mathop{\mathcal{R}\!(A)}, namely the ΔXi\Delta_{X_{i}} and the ΔX−1​ΔX∪{s}\Delta_{X}^{-1}\Delta_{X\cup\{s\}}. We are going to see that this is a general fact; we need first to study the quasi-centralizer of a Garside group.

4.1. The quasi-centralizer

Definition 4.4 (Quasi-centralizer).

Let G+G^{\scriptscriptstyle+} be a Garside monoid with GG as Garside group. The quasi-centralizer of the monoid G+G^{\scriptscriptstyle+} is the submonoid QZ(G+)\mathop{\rm QZ}(G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}) defined by

QZ(G+)={g∈G+∣g​G+=G+​g};\mathop{\rm QZ}(G^{\scriptscriptstyle+})=\{g\in G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\mid gG^{\scriptscriptstyle+}=G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}g\};

The quasi-centralizer of the group GG is the subgroup QZ(G)\mathop{\rm QZ}(G) defined by

QZ(G)={g∈G∣g​G+=G+​g}.\mathop{\rm QZ}(G)=\{g\in G\mid gG^{\scriptscriptstyle+}=G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}g\}.

In other words, QZ(G+)\mathop{\rm QZ}(G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}) and Q​Z​(G)QZ(G) are equal to ℛG+→G++\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\to G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}} and ℛG→G\mathcal{R}_{G\to G}, respectively.

By definition, the Garside element Δ\Delta belongs to QZ(G+)\mathop{\rm QZ}(G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}). In this section, we extend the main result of [22] into every Garside group. The proof is in the spirit of the latter reference. However, some definitions and technical arguments of the proof of [22] cannot be simply extended to every Garside group. This is because in general the set of divisors of Δ\Delta is not finite. In our proof, this argument is replaced by the noetherianity property of G+G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}. We need some preliminary results.

Lemma 4.5.

Let (G+,Δ)(G^{\scriptscriptstyle+},\Delta) be a monoidal Garside structure.
(i) For every gg in G+G^{\scriptscriptstyle+} the set {h−1​(h∨g)∣h∈G+}\{h^{-1}(h\lor g)\mid h\in G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\} has a lcm Δg\Delta_{g} for the left-divisibility. Furthermore, gg left-divides Δg\Delta_{g} and G+​Δg⊆g​G+G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\Delta_{g}\subseteq gG^{\scriptscriptstyle+}.
(ii) For every gg in G+G^{\scriptscriptstyle+} the set {(h​∨~​g)​h−1∣h∈G+}\{(h\tilde{\lor}g)h^{-1}\mid h\in G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\} has a Δ~g\tilde{\Delta}_{g} for the right-divisibility. Furthermore, gg right-divides Δ~g\tilde{\Delta}_{g} and Δ~g​G+⊆G+​g\tilde{\Delta}_{g}G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\subseteq G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}g.

Proof.

By symmetry, it is enough to prove (i)(i). From the noetherianity property of G+G^{\scriptscriptstyle+} it follows that every none-empty subset of G+G^{\scriptscriptstyle+} that has a common multiple for the left-divisibility has a lcm for the left-divisibility. But Δ\Delta is quasi-central and there exists a positive integer nn such that gg left-divides Δn\Delta^{n}. Therefore, Δn\Delta^{n} is a common multiple of {h−1​(h∨g)∣h∈G+}\{h^{-1}(h\lor g)\mid h\in G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\}, and therefore Δg\Delta_{g} exists. By definition we have G+​Δg⊆g​G+G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\Delta_{g}\subseteq gG^{\scriptscriptstyle+}. Finally, considering h=1h=1, we obtain that gg left-divides Δg\Delta_{g}. ∎

Lemma 4.6.

Let (G+,Δ)(G^{\scriptscriptstyle+},\Delta) be a monoidal Garside structure and gg lie in G+G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}.
Define (τ⁡(n))n∈ℕ(\tau(n))_{n\in\mathbb{N}} by τ⁡(0)=g\tau(0)=g,  τ⁡(2​n+1)=Δτ⁡(2​n)\tau(2n+1)=\Delta_{\tau(2n)} and τ⁡(2​n+2)=Δ~τ⁡(2​n+1)\tau(2n+2)=\tilde{\Delta}_{\tau(2n+1)}. The sequence (τ⁡(n))n∈ℕ(\tau(n))_{n\in\mathbb{N}} stabilizes to an element τg\tau_{g} which belongs to Q​Z​(G+)QZ(G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}). Furthermore, for every element hh in Q​Z​(G+)QZ(G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}), gg left-divides hh if and only if τg\tau_{g} left-divides hh. In particular, for every quasi-central element hh, we have τh=h\tau_{h}=h.

When the set of divisors of Δ\Delta is finite, then one has τg=τ⁡(1)=Δg\tau_{g}=\tau(1)=\Delta_{g} [22].

Proof.

By the previous lemma, τ⁡(2​n+1)\tau(2n+1) left-divides τ⁡(2​n)\tau(2n), and τ⁡(2​n+2)\tau(2n+2) right-divides τ⁡(2​n+1)\tau(2n+1). Furthermore, with the notation of Lemma 4.5’s proof, all the τn\tau_{n} divides Δn\Delta^{n} (for both the left-divisibility and the right-divisibility since Δn\Delta^{n} is a quasi-central element). By the noetherianity property, there exist Δg\Delta_{g} in G+G^{\scriptscriptstyle+} and N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N} such that τ⁡(n)=τg\tau(n)=\tau_{g} for every n≥Nn\geq N. By Lemma 4.5, we get the sequence of inclusions τ⁡(2​n+2)​G+⊆G+​τ​(2​n+1)⊆τ⁡(2​n)​G+\tau(2n+2)G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\subseteq G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\tau(2n+1)\subseteq\tau(2n)G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}. Thus, τg\tau_{g} is a quasi-central element. Assume hh lies in Q​Z​(G+)QZ(G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}) such that gg left-divides hh, and write h=g​g′h=gg^{\prime}. By assumption, we have G+​h=h​G+=g​g′​G+G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}h=hG^{\scriptscriptstyle+}=gg^{\prime}G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}. Therefore, hh is a common multiple of the set {k−1​(k∨g)∣k∈G+}\{k^{-1}(k\lor g)\mid k\in G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\} and Δg\Delta_{g} left-divides hh. But hh is quasi-central, then Δg\Delta_{g}, that is τ⁡(1)\tau(1), also right-divides hh. Inductively we get that τ⁡(n)\tau(n) left-divides and right-divides hh for every nn. Finally, by Lemma 4.5, τ⁡(2​n)\tau(2n) left-divides τ⁡(2​n+1)\tau(2n+1) and τ⁡(2​n+1)\tau(2n+1) right-divides τ⁡(2​n+2)\tau(2n+2) for every nn; then we can write τg=g1​g​g2\tau_{g}=g_{1}gg_{2} for some g1,g2g_{1},g_{2} in G+G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}. Since τg\tau_{g} is a quasi-central, it follows that gg left-divides τg\tau_{g}. ∎

Remark 4.7.

With the notation of Lemma 4.6 and a similar proof of this lemma, we can obtain an element τ~g\tilde{\tau}_{g} by considering the sequence (τ~​(n))n∈ℕ(\tilde{\tau}(n))_{n\in\mathbb{N}} defined by τ~​(0)=g\tilde{\tau}(0)=g,  τ~​(2​n+1)=Δ~τ~​(2​n)\tilde{\tau}(2n+1)=\tilde{\Delta}_{\tilde{\tau}(2n)} and τ~​(2​n+2)=Δτ⁡(2​n+1)\tilde{\tau}(2n+2)=\Delta_{\tau(2n+1)}. Using that an element of QZ(G+)\mathop{\rm QZ}(G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}) has the same set of left-divisors and of right-divisors, we deduce that τg=τ~g\tau_{g}=\tilde{\tau}_{g} for every gg in G+G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}.

Proposition 4.8.

Let (G+,Δ)(G^{\scriptscriptstyle+},\Delta) be a monoidal Garside structure, and denote by SS the atom set of G+G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}. For every s,ts,t in SS, either τs=τt\tau_{s}=\tau_{t} or τs∧τt=τs​∧~​τt=1\tau_{s}\!\wedge\!\tau_{t}=\tau_{s}\tilde{\wedge}\tau_{t}=1 in G+G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}. Furthermore, in any case, τs​τt=τt​τs\tau_{s}\tau_{t}=\tau_{t}\tau_{s}.

Proof.

The main argument of the first part’s proof is as in [22]. Since τt\tau_{t} is a quasi-central element, it has the same left-divisors and right-divisors. Assume that ss divides τt\tau_{t} and let us prove that τs=τt\tau_{s}=\tau_{t}. By Lemma 4.6, we can write τt=h​τs=g​t\tau_{t}=h\tau_{s}=gt. Still by Lemma 4.6, if tt divides τs\tau_{s}, then τt\tau_{t} divides τs\tau_{s} and we are done: τs=τt\tau_{s}=\tau_{t}. Assume this is not the case. Since tt is an atom of G+G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}, the elements gg and τs\tau_{s} are prime to each other for the right-divisibility in G+G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}. This implies that τt\tau_{t} is the lcm of gg and hh for the left-divisibility. In particular, t=g−1​(h∨g)t=g^{-1}(h\lor g). Then, by definition, tt left-divides Δh\Delta_{h} and, therefore, left-divides τh\tau_{h}. In particular, we can write τh=τt​k\tau_{h}=\tau_{t}k for some kk in G+G^{+}. But τs\tau_{s} and τt\tau_{t} are quasi-central elements, then hh is also a quasi-central element and h=τhh=\tau_{h}. A contradiction: we get τt=h​τs=τh​τs=τt​k​τs\tau_{t}=h\tau_{s}=\tau_{h}\tau_{s}=\tau_{t}k\tau_{s} with τs≠1\tau_{s}\neq 1. Now, if τs∧τt≠1\tau_{s}\!\wedge\!\tau_{t}\neq 1 then there exists uu in SS that divides both τs\tau_{s} and τt\tau_{t}. By the above argument, we have τs=τu=τt\tau_{s}=\tau_{u}=\tau_{t}.

Assume finally that τs≠τt\tau_{s}\neq\tau_{t}. We can write τs​τt=τt​g1=g2​τs\tau_{s}\tau_{t}=\tau_{t}g_{1}=g_{2}\tau_{s} and τt​τs=τs​h1=h2​τt\tau_{t}\tau_{s}=\tau_{s}h_{1}=h_{2}\tau_{t} where g1,g2,h1,h2g_{1},g_{2},h_{1},h_{2} lie in G+G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}. Clearly g1,g2,h1,h2g_{1},g_{2},h_{1},h_{2} have to be quasi-central elements. As τt≠τs\tau_{t}\neq\tau_{s}, by the first part of the proof, the decomposition τt−1​τs\tau_{t}^{-1}\tau_{s} is a left greedy normal form (cf. Prop. 2.6(i​i)(ii)). But we have τt−1​τs=g1​τt−1=τs​h1−1\tau_{t}^{-1}\tau_{s}=g_{1}\tau_{t}^{-1}=\tau_{s}h_{1}^{-1}. Since τt−1​τs\tau_{t}^{-1}\tau_{s} is not in G+G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}, τt\tau_{t} and τs\tau_{s} do not right-divide g1g_{1} and h1h_{1}, respectively. This implies that both g1​τt−1g_{1}\tau_{t}^{-1} and τs​h1−1\tau_{s}h_{1}^{-1} are right greedy normal forms. By unicity of this normal form, we get g1=τsg_{1}=\tau_{s} and h1=τth_{1}=\tau_{t}. Thus, τs​τt=τt​τs\tau_{s}\tau_{t}=\tau_{t}\tau_{s}. ∎

Theorem 4.9.

Let (G+,Δ)(G^{\scriptscriptstyle+},\Delta) be a monoidal Garside structure, and denote by SS the atom set of G+G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}.
(i) The monoid Q​Z​(G+)QZ(G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}) is a free commutative monoid. Furthermore there exists a projection τ:G+→QZ(G+),g↦τg\tau:G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\to\mathop{\rm QZ}(G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}),\ g\mapsto\tau_{g} such that

  1. (1)

    the set {τs∣s∈S}\{\tau_{s}\mid s\in S\} is a free base of QZ(G+)\mathop{\rm QZ}(G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}) (where some τs\tau_{s} are possibly equal);

  2. (2)

    the map τ\tau respects the left-divisibility and the right-divisibility, in particular if s∈Ss\in S left/right-divides g∈QZ(G+)g\in\mathop{\rm QZ}(G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}) then τs\tau_{s} left/right-divides gg;

  3. (3)

    the map τ\tau is a semilattice homomorphism for ∨\lor and for ∨~\tilde{\lor}; in particular, τg∨h=τg∨τh\tau_{g\lor h}=\tau_{g}\lor\tau_{h} for every g,hg,h in G+G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}.

(ii) The group Q​Z​(G)QZ(G) is a free commutative group with {τs∣s∈S}\{\tau_{s}\mid s\in S\} as a free base (where some τs\tau_{s} are possibly equal).

This theorem should be compared with the definition of ν\nu-functions (cf. Definition 3.12). Note that the map τ\tau is not a semilattice homomorphism for ∧\land (nor ∧~\tilde{\land} ) in general [22].

Proof.

(i)(i) We already know by Lemma 4.6 that τ⁡(QZ(G+))=QZ(G+)\tau(\mathop{\rm QZ}(G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}))=\mathop{\rm QZ}(G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}), that τ2=τ\tau^{2}=\tau and that τ\tau respects the left-divisibility and the right-divisibility. Furthermore, using the noetherianity property and the same lemma, we get that the set {τs∣s∈S}\{\tau_{s}\mid s\in S\} is a generating set for QZ(G+)\mathop{\rm QZ}(G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}). By Proposition 4.8, it follows that the monoid QZ(G+)\mathop{\rm QZ}(G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}) is commutative, and that for distinct elements τs\tau_{s} and τt\tau_{t}, the element τs​τt\tau_{s}\tau_{t} is a common multiple of τs\tau_{s} and τt\tau_{t} for both the left-divisibility and the right-divisibility. Using Lemma 4.6, we get that τs​τt\tau_{s}\tau_{t} is the lcm of τs\tau_{s} and τt\tau_{t} (for both the left-divisibility and the right-divisibility): otherwise, there would be some uu in SS that divides both τs\tau_{s} and τt\tau_{t} and then we should have τs=τu=τt\tau_{s}=\tau_{u}=\tau_{t}. Therefore, Q​Z​(G+)QZ(G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}) is a free commutative monoid with {τs∣s∈S}\{\tau_{s}\mid s\in S\} as a free base. Now, let gg and hh belong to G+G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}. They left-divides g∨hg\lor h. Therefore τg\tau_{g}, τh\tau_{h} and τg∨τh\tau_{g}\lor\tau_{h} left-divides τg∨h\tau_{g\lor h}. But τg\tau_{g} and τh\tau_{h} have a common multiple in QZ(G+)\mathop{\rm QZ}(G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}) for the left-divisibility (that is some power of Δ\Delta). By the noetherianity property, there exists a minimal common multiple τg​g′=τh​h′\tau_{g}g^{\prime}=\tau_{h}h^{\prime} of τs\tau_{s} and τt\tau_{t} for the left-divisibility in Q​Z​(G+)QZ(G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}). Assume there exists uu in SS that right-divides both g′g^{\prime} and h′h^{\prime}; then by Remark 4.7, τu\tau_{u} also right-divides g′g^{\prime} and h′h^{\prime}, which is impossible by minimality. Therefore τg∨τh\tau_{g}\lor\tau_{h} belongs to QZ(G+)\mathop{\rm QZ}(G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}). Since g∨hg\lor h left-divides τg∨τh\tau_{g}\lor\tau_{h}, the element τg∨h\tau_{g\lor h} left-divides τg∨τh\tau_{g}\lor\tau_{h}. As a conclusion, τg∨h\tau_{g\lor h} is equal to τg∨τh\tau_{g}\lor\tau_{h}.
(i​i)(ii) Let gg lie in QZ(G)\mathop{\rm QZ}(G) and a−1​ba^{-1}b be its left greedy normal form (cf. Proposition 2.6). We claim that aa and bb belong to QZ(G+)\mathop{\rm QZ}(G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}). This proves that QZ(G)\mathop{\rm QZ}(G) is (isomorphic to) the group of fractions of QZ(G+)\mathop{\rm QZ}(G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}) and, therefore, the second point of the proposition. Actually, every element gg of GG can be written as Δ−n​g+\Delta^{-n}g^{\scriptscriptstyle+} with n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} and g+g^{\scriptscriptstyle+} in G+G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}. But Δ\Delta is a quasi-central element. Therefore, when gg lies in QZ(G)\mathop{\rm QZ}(G), then g+g^{\scriptscriptstyle+} and Δn\Delta^{n} belong to QZ(G+)\mathop{\rm QZ}(G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}). Now assume that g=c−1​dg=c^{-1}d where both cc and dd lie in QZ(G+)\mathop{\rm QZ}(G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}). If some uu in SS left-divides both cc and dd, then τu\tau_{u} also left-divides cc and dd. We conclude as in the proof of (i)(i). ∎

In the next section, we are going to apply the above results to parabolic submonoids. We recall that we have fixed a Garside monoid A+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+} with a ν\nu-structure in the introduction of Section 4.

Corollary 4.10.

Let G+=AX+G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}=A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{X} be a parabolic submonoid of A+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}. Let ss belong to SS.
(i) If ss lies in XX, then τs=νX​(s)\tau_{s}=\nu_{X}(s);
(ii) If νX​(s)\nu_{X}(s) belongs to AX+A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}, then there exists tt in XX such that νX​(s)=τt\nu_{X}(s)=\tau_{t}.

Proof.

(i)(i) Assume ss lies in XX. Since ss left-divides τs\tau_{s}, by the defining properties of a ν\nu-structure, νX​(s)\nu_{X}(s) left-divides τs\tau_{s}. But τs\tau_{s} belongs to AX+A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+} which is a parabolic submonoid. Therefore, νX​(s)\nu_{X}(s) belongs to AX+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{X}. Consequently, νX​(s)\nu_{X}(s) lies in QZ(AX+)\mathop{\rm QZ}(A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}), and has to be equal to τs\tau_{s}.
(i​i)(ii) Assume νX​(s)\nu_{X}(s) belongs to AX+A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}. This implies that νX​(s)\nu_{X}(s) lies in QZ(AX+)\mathop{\rm QZ}(A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}), and therefore is equal to a product τt1⋯τtk\tau_{t_{1}}\cdots\tau_{t_{k}} with t1,…,tkt_{1},\ldots,t_{k} in SS. But νX​(s)\nu_{X}(s) is an atom of ℛ+​(A+)\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}, hence k=1k=1. ∎

4.2. Defining relations

We still consider the general notations of Section 4. In Lemma 4.3, we have seen that the quiver 𝒜\mathcal{A} whose edges are the νX​(s)\nu_{X}(s) is a generating quiver for the groupoid ℛ⁡(A)\mathop{\mathcal{R}\!(A)}. In Corollary 4.10, we have seen that among the νX​(s)\nu_{X}(s) there is two kinds of atoms of ℛ+​(A+)\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}, like in the case of Artin-Tits groups of spherical type (cf. Example 3.14). In the sequel, for every parabolic submonoid G+=AX+G^{\scriptscriptstyle+}=A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+} of A+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}, and every element ss that belongs to SS, we denote by τ⁡(X,s)\tau(X,s) the element νX​(s)\nu_{X}(s) when it belongs to AX+A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}, and by ν⁡(X,s)\nu(X,s) otherwise. Similarly, we write τ~​(X,s)\tilde{\tau}(X,s) or ν~​(X,s)\tilde{\nu}(X,s) for ν~X​(s)\tilde{\nu}_{X}(s), depending whether or not this atom lies in AX+A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}. For instance, for every ss in XX, one has τs=τ⁡(X,s)=νX​(s)\tau_{s}=\tau(X,s)=\nu_{X}(s).

Lemma 4.11.

Let AX+A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+} and AY+A_{Y}^{\scriptscriptstyle+} be parabolic submonoids of A+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}. Assume τ⁡(X,s)\tau(X,s) lies in QZ(AX+)\mathop{\rm QZ}(A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}) and ν⁡(X,t)\nu(X,t) belongs to ℛ+​(A+)AX+→AY+\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}_{A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\to A_{Y}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}}. Then, there exists τ⁡(Y,s′)\tau(Y,s^{\prime}) in QZ(AY+)\mathop{\rm QZ}(A_{Y}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}) such that

(†) τ⁡(X,s)​ν​(X,t)=ν⁡(X,t)​τ​(Y,s′).\tau(X,s)\nu(X,t)=\nu(X,t)\tau(Y,s^{\prime}).
Proof.

Since τ⁡(X,s)\tau(X,s) lies in QZ(AX+)\mathop{\rm QZ}(A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}) and ν⁡(X,t)\nu(X,t) belongs to ℛ+​(A+)AX+→AY+\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}_{A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\to A_{Y}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}}, the element ν​(X,t)−1​τ​(X,s)​ν​(X,t)\nu(X,t)^{-1}\tau(X,s)\nu(X,t) belongs to QZ(AY+)\mathop{\rm QZ}(A_{Y}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}). But τ⁡(X,s)\tau(X,s) is an atom of the category ℛ+​(A+)\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}. Therefore ν​(X,t)−1​τ​(X,s)​ν​(X,t)\nu(X,t)^{-1}\tau(X,s)\nu(X,t) is also an atom of ℛ+​(A+)\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}. By Corollary 4.10, we are done. ∎

When proving Lemma 4.13 and Theorem 4.14 we will use the following result:

Lemma 4.12.

Let AX+A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+} and AY+A_{Y}^{\scriptscriptstyle+} be parabolic submonoids of A+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}. Assume that gg is equal to ν(X1,s1)⋯ν(Xk,sk)\nu(X_{1},s_{1})\cdots\nu(X_{k},s_{k}) and lies in ℛ+​(A+)AX+→AY+\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}_{A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\to A_{Y}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}}, where X1=XX_{1}=X; assume furthermore that h1h_{1} belongs to AX+A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+} and h2h_{2} belongs to AY+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{Y}. Then,
(i) the lcm and the gcd in A+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+} of gg and h1h_{1} for the left-divisibility is h1​gh_{1}g and 11, respectively.
(ii) the lcm and the gcd in A+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+} of gg and h2h_{2} for the right-divisibility is g​h2gh_{2} and 11, respectively.

Proof.

Assume k=1k=1. If uu in SS left-divides both gg and h1h_{1}, then uu lies in XX and τ⁡(X,u)\tau(X,u) left-divides ν⁡(X,s)\nu(X,s). This is impossible because in this case we would have ν⁡(X,s)=τ⁡(X,u)\nu(X,s)=\tau(X,u). Therefore, the gcd in A+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}of gg and h1h_{1} for the left-divisibility is 11. Similarly, the gcd of gg in A+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+} and h2h_{2} for the right-divisibility is 11 (We recall that ν⁡(X,t)\nu(X,t) is equal to some ν~​(Y,s)\tilde{\nu}(Y,s)). Let h2′h^{\prime}_{2} in AX+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{X} be such that h2′​g=g​h2h^{\prime}_{2}g=gh_{2}. The gcd of h2′h^{\prime}_{2} and gg for the left-divisibility is 11 by the first part of the proof. Thus, g​h2gh_{2} is the lcm of gg and h2h_{2} for the right-divisibility. Similarly, h1​gh_{1}g is the lcm in A+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+} of gg and h1h_{1} for the left-divisibility.

Assume k≥2k\geq 2. By an easy induction on kk we deduce from the case k=1k=1 that the element h1​gh_{1}g is the lcm of gg and h1h_{1} for the left-divisibility. Similarly g​h2gh_{2} is the lcm of gg and h2h_{2} for the right-divisibility. Finally, we deduce from the latter result the last part of the lemma: let h1′h^{\prime}_{1} be the gcd of gg and h1h_{1} for the left-divisibility. Since AX+A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+} is a parabolic submonoid, h1′h^{\prime}_{1} belongs to AX+A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}. In particular the lcm of h1′h^{\prime}_{1} and gg for the left-divisibility, which is gg, has to be equal to h1′​gh^{\prime}_{1}g. Then h1′=1h^{\prime}_{1}=1. Similarly, the gcd of gg and h2h_{2} for the right-divisibility is 11. ∎

We recall that the quiver 𝒜\mathcal{A} has been defined in Lemma 4.3, and that we can have νX​(s)=νX​(t)\nu_{X}(s)=\nu_{X}(t) in the quiver 𝒜\mathcal{A}, even though s≠ts\neq t.

Lemma 4.13.

Let AX+A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+} be a parabolic submonoid of A+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+} and consider AY+A_{Y}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}, AZ+A_{Z}^{\scriptscriptstyle+} two parabolic submonoids of A+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+} which are distinct from AX+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{X}. Assume ν⁡(X,s)\nu(X,s) and ν⁡(X,t)\nu(X,t) belong to ℛ+​(A+)AX+→AY+\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}_{A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\to A_{Y}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}} and ℛ+​(A+)AX+→AZ+\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}_{A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\to A_{Z}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}}, respectively. Then, there exist a parabolic submonoid AX′+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{X^{\prime}}, a path ν(Y1,s1)⋯ν(Yk,sk)\nu(Y_{1},s_{1})\cdots\nu(Y_{k},s_{k}) in 𝒞​(𝒜)AY+→AX′+\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{A})_{A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{Y}\to A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{X^{\prime}}} and a path ν(Z1,t1)⋯ν(Zℓ,tℓ)\nu(Z_{1},t_{1})\cdots\nu(Z_{\ell},t_{\ell}) in 𝒞​(𝒜)AZ+→AX′+\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{A})_{A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{Z}\to A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{X^{\prime}}} such that

(‡) ν(X,s)∨ν(X,t)=ν(X,s)ν(Y1,s1)⋯ν(Yk,sk)=ν(X,t)ν(Z1,t1)⋯ν(Zℓ,tℓ).\nu(X,s)\lor\nu(X,t)=\nu(X,s)\nu(Y_{1},s_{1})\cdots\nu(Y_{k},s_{k})=\nu(X,t)\nu(Z_{1},t_{1})\cdots\nu(Z_{\ell},t_{\ell}).
Proof.

We can assume ν⁡(X,s)≠ν⁡(X,t)\nu(X,s)\neq\nu(X,t). The category ℛ+​(A+)\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})} is a Garside category with 𝒜\mathcal{A} for atom graph. Then we can decompose ν⁡(X,s)∨ν⁡(X,t)\nu(X,s)\lor\nu(X,t) in  the category ℛ+​(A+)\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}:

ν(X,s)∨ν(X,t)=ν(X,s)νY1(s1)⋯νYk(sk)=ν(X,t)νZ1(t1)⋯νZℓ(tℓ).\nu(X,s)\lor\nu(X,t)=\nu(X,s)\nu_{Y_{1}}(s_{1})\cdots\nu_{Y_{k}}(s_{k})=\nu(X,t)\nu_{Z_{1}}(t_{1})\cdots\nu_{Z_{\ell}}(t_{\ell}).

By Lemma 4.11, we can assume without restriction that there exists k1k_{1} and ℓ1\ell_{1} such that νYi​(si)\nu_{Y_{i}}(s_{i}) is equal to ν⁡(Yi,si)\nu(Y_{i},s_{i}) if and only if i≤k1i\leq k_{1}, and that νZi​(ti)\nu_{Z_{i}}(t_{i}) is equal to ν⁡(Zi,ti)\nu(Z_{i},t_{i}) if and only if i≤ℓ1i\leq\ell_{1}. Let us set g=νYk1+1(sk1+1)⋯νYk(sk)g=\nu_{Y_{k_{1}+1}}\!(s_{k_{1}+1})\cdots\nu_{Y_{k}}(s_{k}) and h=νZℓ1+1(tℓ1+1)⋯νZℓ(tℓ)h=\nu_{Z_{\ell_{1}+1}}(t_{\ell_{1}+1})\cdots\nu_{Z_{\ell}}(t_{\ell}), and consider g1,h1g_{1},h_{1} such that g​∨~​h=g1​g=h1​hg\tilde{\lor}h=g_{1}g=h_{1}h. Since gg and hh belong to AY+A_{Y}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}, the elements g1g_{1} and h1h_{1} lie in AY+A_{Y}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}. But g1g_{1} has to right-divide ν(X,s)νY1(s1)⋯νYk1(sk1)\nu(X,s)\nu_{Y_{1}}(s_{1})\cdots\nu_{Y_{k_{1}}}(s_{k_{1}}). Then, by Lemma 4.12, we have g1=1g_{1}=1. Similarly, h1=1h_{1}=1 that is g=hg=h. Finally we get g=h=1g=h=1 since the lcm of gg and hh for the right-divisibility has to be 11. ∎

Theorem 4.14.

Let (A+,Δ)(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+},\Delta) be a monoidal Garside structure with a ν\nu-structure. Denote by SS the atom set of (A+𝐶𝐿𝑂𝑆𝐸(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}, and by AA its group of fractions. Consider the set RR of equalities of paths in 𝒞⁡(𝒜)\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{A}):

  1. (1)

    τ⁡(X,s)​τ​(X,t)=τ⁡(X,t)​τ​(X,s)\tau(X,s)\tau(X,t)=\tau(X,t)\tau(X,s);

  2. (2)

    τ⁡(X,s)​ν​(X,t)=ν⁡(X,t)​τ​(Y,s′)\tau(X,s)\nu(X,t)=\nu(X,t)\tau(Y,s^{\prime});

  3. (3)

    ν(X,s)ν(Y1,s1)⋯ν(Yk,sk)=ν(X,t)ν(Z1,t1)⋯ν(Zℓ,tℓ)\nu(X,s)\nu(Y_{1},s_{1})\cdots\nu(Y_{k},s_{k})=\nu(X,t)\nu(Z_{1},t_{1})\cdots\nu(Z_{\ell},t_{\ell})

that hold in ℛ+​(A+)\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})} and such that in Equalities of type (3) the two paths correspond to two decompositions of ν⁡(X,s)∨ν⁡(X,t)\nu(X,s)\lor\nu(X,t) as in Equation (‡ ‣ 4.13) of Lemma 4.13.
Then, ⟨𝒜,R⟩\langle\mathcal{A},R\rangle is a presentation of ℛ⁡(A)\mathop{\mathcal{R}\!(A)} as a groupoid.

Proof.

The Garside group AA has a ν\nu-function, then ℛ⁡(A)\mathop{\mathcal{R}\!(A)} is a Garside groupoid, with ℛ+​(A+)\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})} as Garside category. Therefore, it is enough to prove that ⟨𝒜,R⟩\langle\mathcal{A},R\rangle is a presentation of ℛ+​(A+)\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})} as a category. We already know that 𝒜\mathcal{A} is a generating quiver of ℛ+​(A+)\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}. Now, let ≡\equiv be the congruence on ℳ⁡(𝒜)\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{A}) defined by the relations considered in the theorem. Let νY1(s1)⋯νYk(sk)\nu_{Y_{1}}(s_{1})\cdots\nu_{Y_{k}}(s_{k}) and νZ1(t1)⋯νZℓ(tℓ)\nu_{Z_{1}}(t_{1})\cdots\nu_{Z_{\ell}}(t_{\ell}) be two paths in 𝒞​(𝒜)AX+→AX′+\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{A})_{A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\to A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{X^{\prime}}}. Clearly, if the two paths are ≡\equiv-equivalent, they represent the same element in ℛ+​(A+)AX+→AX′+\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}_{A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\to A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{X^{\prime}}}. Conversely, assume they represent the same element in ℛ+​(A+)AX+→AX′+\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}_{A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\to A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{X^{\prime}}} and let us prove that they are ≡\equiv-equivalent. Using defining relations (2) of ≡\equiv, we obtain a path ν(Y1′,s1′)⋯ν(Yk1′,sk1′)τ(X′,sk1+1′)⋯τ(X′,sk′)\nu(Y^{\prime}_{1},s^{\prime}_{1})\cdots\nu(Y^{\prime}_{k_{1}},s^{\prime}_{k_{1}})\tau(X^{\prime},s^{\prime}_{k_{1}+1})\cdots\tau(X^{\prime},s^{\prime}_{k}) which is  ≡\equiv-equivalent to the path νY1(s1)⋯νYk(sk)\nu_{Y_{1}}(s_{1})\cdots\nu_{Y_{k}}(s_{k}). Similarly, we also obtain a path ν(Z1′,t1′)⋯ν(Zℓ1′,tℓ1′)τ(X′,tℓ1+1′)⋯τ(X′,tℓ′)\nu(Z^{\prime}_{1},t^{\prime}_{1})\cdots\nu(Z^{\prime}_{\ell_{1}},t^{\prime}_{\ell_{1}})\tau(X^{\prime},t^{\prime}_{\ell_{1}+1})\cdots\tau(X^{\prime},t^{\prime}_{\ell}) which is  ≡\equiv-equivalent to the path νZ1(t1)⋯νZℓ(tℓ)\nu_{Z_{1}}(t_{1})\cdots\nu_{Z_{\ell}}(t_{\ell}). By Lemma 4.12 the equalities ν(Y1′,s1′)⋯ν(Yk1′,sk1′)=ν(Z1′,t1′)⋯ν(Zℓ1′,tℓ1′)\nu(Y^{\prime}_{1},s^{\prime}_{1})\cdots\nu(Y^{\prime}_{k_{1}},s^{\prime}_{k_{1}})=\nu(Z^{\prime}_{1},t^{\prime}_{1})\cdots\nu(Z^{\prime}_{\ell_{1}},t^{\prime}_{\ell_{1}}) and τ(X′,sk1+1′)⋯τ(X′,sk′)=τ(X′,tℓ1+1′)⋯τ(X′,tℓ′)\tau(X^{\prime},s^{\prime}_{k_{1}+1})\cdots\tau(X^{\prime},s^{\prime}_{k})=\tau(X^{\prime},t^{\prime}_{\ell_{1}+1})\cdots\tau(X^{\prime},t^{\prime}_{\ell}) hold in A+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+} (see the proof of Lemma 4.13). From Theorem 4.9, it follows that the two paths τ(X′,sk1+1′)⋯τ(X′,sk′)\tau(X^{\prime},s^{\prime}_{k_{1}+1})\cdots\tau(X^{\prime},s^{\prime}_{k}) and τ(X′,tℓ1+1′)⋯τ(X′,tℓ′)\tau(X^{\prime},t^{\prime}_{\ell_{1}+1})\cdots\tau(X^{\prime},t^{\prime}_{\ell}) are ≡\equiv-equivalent, using the relations of type (1). Finally, ν(Y1′,s1′)⋯ν(Yk1′,sk1′)\nu(Y^{\prime}_{1},s^{\prime}_{1})\cdots\nu(Y^{\prime}_{k_{1}},s^{\prime}_{k_{1}}) and ν(Z1′,t1′)⋯ν(Zℓ1′,tℓ1′)\nu(Z^{\prime}_{1},t^{\prime}_{1})\cdots\nu(Z^{\prime}_{\ell_{1}},t^{\prime}_{\ell_{1}}) are ≡\equiv-equivalent by Lemma 4.16. Define XX to be the set made of the paths in 𝒞​(𝒜)⋅→AX′+\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{A})_{\cdot\to A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{X^{\prime}}} whose images in ℛ+​(A+)⋅→AX′+\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}_{\cdot\to A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{X^{\prime}}} right-divides ν(Y1′,s1′)⋯ν(Yk1′,sk1′)\nu(Y^{\prime}_{1},s^{\prime}_{1})\cdots\nu(Y^{\prime}_{k_{1}},s^{\prime}_{k_{1}}). We define a noetherian partial order on XX by saying that for ω1,ω2\omega_{1},\omega_{2} in XX, one has ω1≤ω2\omega_{1}\leq\omega_{2} if ω1=ω2\omega_{1}=\omega_{2} in 𝒞​(𝒜)⋅→AX′+\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{A})_{\cdot\to A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{X^{\prime}}}, or the image of ω1\omega_{1} in ℛ+​(A+)\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})} strictly right-divides the image of ω2\omega_{2}. We fix for every element ww in ℛ+​(A+)⋅→AX′+\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}_{\cdot\to A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{X^{\prime}}} a representing path w^\hat{w} in 𝒞​(𝒜)⋅→AX′+\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{A})_{\cdot\to A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{X^{\prime}}}. Remark 4.15.

Given a Garside monoid with a right partial action on a set, Dehornoy shows in [9] that under a technical hypothesis, a natural Garside category can be associated with this action. We note that the positive ribbon category ℛ+​(A+)\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})} does not arised trivially in this way. Actually, we can not defined a right partial action of A+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+} on the set of its parabolic submonoids by setting for an atom ss that AX+⋅s=AY+A_{X}^{+}\cdot s=A_{Y}^{+} where YY is such that νX​(s)\nu_{X}(s) belongs to ℛ+​(A+)AX+→AY+\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}_{A_{X}^{+}\to A_{Y}^{+}}. For instance, consider the braid group B4B_{4} with the notations of Example 2.3; then (A{s2}+⋅s1)⋅s3=A{s1}(A_{\{s_{2}\}}^{+}\cdot s_{1})\cdot s_{3}=A_{\{s_{1}\}} whereas (A{s2}+⋅s3)⋅s1=A{s3}(A_{\{s_{2}\}}^{+}\cdot s_{3})\cdot s_{1}=A_{\{s_{3}\}}. Indeed, we do not have the equality ν{s2}​(s1)​ν{s1}​(s3)=ν{s2}​(s3)​ν{s3}​(s1)\nu_{\{s_{2}\}}\!(s_{1})\,\nu_{\{s_{1}\}}\!(s_{3})=\nu_{\{s_{2}\}}\!(s_{3})\,\nu_{\{s_{3}\}}\!(s_{1}) but

ν{s2}​(s1)​ν{s1}​(s3)​ν{s1}​(s2)=ν{s2}​(s3)​ν{s3}​(s1)​ν{s3}​(s2)\nu_{\{s_{2}\}}\!(s_{1})\,\nu_{\{s_{1}\}}\!(s_{3})\,\nu_{\{s_{1}\}}\!(s_{2})=\nu_{\{s_{2}\}}\!(s_{3})\,\nu_{\{s_{3}\}}\!(s_{1})\,\nu_{\{s_{3}\}}\!(s_{2})

which is a relation of type (3) in Theorem 4.14.

Lemma 4.16.

Let (X,≤)(X,\leq) be a noetherian partially ordered set with an infimum element denoted by 11. Assume EE is a subset of X×XX\times X that contains {(x,x)∣x∈X}\{(x,x)\mid x\in X\} and which is stabilized by the maps (x,y)↦(y,x)(x,y)\mapsto(y,x). Assume ϕ:E→E,(x,y)↦(ϕ1​(x,y),ϕ2​(x,y))\phi:E\to E,(x,y)\mapsto(\phi_{1}(x,y),\phi_{2}(x,y)) is such that ϕ⁡(x,x)=(1,1)\phi(x,x)=(1,1) for xx in EE, and ϕ1​(x,y)<x\phi_{1}(x,y)<x and ϕ2​(x,y)<x\phi_{2}(x,y)<x for x≠yx\neq y. Consider ψn:E→E2n\psi_{n}:E\to E^{2^{n}} defined inductively by ψ0​(x,y)=(x,y)\psi_{0}(x,y)=(x,y) and ψn​(x,y)=(ψn−1​(ϕ⁡(x,y)),ψn−1​(ϕ⁡(y,x)))\psi_{n}(x,y)=(\psi_{n-1}(\phi(x,y)),\psi_{n-1}(\phi(y,x))) for n≥1n\geq 1. For every (x,y)(x,y) in EE, there exists nn such that ψn​(x,y)=(1,1,⋯,1)\psi_{n}(x,y)=(1,1,\cdots,1).

Proof.

If it was not the case, then we could construct a strictly decreasing sequence in XX, which is impossible by the noetherianity property. ∎

In the sequel, we denote by ℛ+ν​(A+)\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+\nu}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})} and ℛν​(A)\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle\nu}\!(A)} the subcategory and the subgroupoid of ℛ+​(A+)\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})} and ℛ⁡(A)\mathop{\mathcal{R}\!(A)}, respectively, generated by the ν⁡(X,s)\nu(X,s).

Lemma 4.17.

(i) For every gg which lies in ℛ+​(A+)AX+→⋅\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}_{A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\to\cdot}, there exists a unique pair (g1,g2)(g_{1},g_{2}) such that g=g1​g2g=g_{1}g_{2} with g1g_{1} in QZ(AX+)\mathop{\rm QZ}(A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}) and g2g_{2} in ℛ+ν​(A+)AX+→⋅\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+\nu}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}_{A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\to\cdot}.
(ii) Let g,hg,h belong to ℛ+​(A+)AX+→⋅\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}_{A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\to\cdot}. Assume g=g1​g2g=g_{1}g_{2} and h=h1​h2h=h_{1}h_{2} with g1,h1g_{1},h_{1} in QZ(AX+)\mathop{\rm QZ}(A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}) and g2,h2g_{2},h_{2} in ℛ+ν​(A+)AX+→⋅\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+\nu}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}_{A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\to\cdot}. Then g∨hg\lor h is equal to (g1∨h1)​(g2∨h2)(g_{1}\lor h_{1})(g_{2}\lor h_{2}), and g∧hg\land his equal to (g1∧h1)​(g2∧h2)(g_{1}\land h_{1})(g_{2}\land h_{2}).

Proof.

(i)(i) it has been proved when proving Theorem 4.14.
(i​i)(ii) It is clear that (g1∨h1)​(g2∨h2)(g_{1}\lor h_{1})(g_{2}\lor h_{2}) is a common multiple of gg and hh. Conversely, any common multiple of gg and hh is a common multiple of (g1∨h1)(g_{1}\lor h_{1}) and (g2∨h2)(g_{2}\lor h_{2}) for the left-divisibility. But the lcm of the latter is (g1∨h1)​(g2∨h2)(g_{1}\lor h_{1})(g_{2}\lor h_{2}) by Lemma 4.12 (the lcm of g2g_{2} and h2h_{2} lies in ℛ+​(A+)AX+→⋅\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}_{A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\to\cdot} by Lemma 4.13). Similarly, (g1∧h1)​(g2∧h2)(g_{1}\land h_{1})(g_{2}\land h_{2}) is a common left-divisor of gg and hh. Now, let k=k1​k2k=k_{1}k_{2} belong to ℛ+​(A+)AX+→⋅\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}_{A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\to\cdot} with k1k_{1} in QZ(AX+)\mathop{\rm QZ}(A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}) and k2k_{2} in ℛ+ν​(A+)AX+→⋅\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+\nu}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}_{A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\to\cdot}, and assume kk left-divides both gg and hh. Using that gg is the lcm of gg and kk for the left-divisibility, we get that k1k_{1} and k2k_{2} left-divide g1g_{1} and g2g_{2}, respectively. By the same argument, k1k_{1} and k2k_{2} also left-divide h1h_{1} and h2h_{2}, respectively. We deduce that k1k_{1} and k2k_{2} left-divide (g1∧h1)(g_{1}\land h_{1}) and (g2∧h2)(g_{2}\land h_{2}), and finally that kk left-divides (g1∧h1)​(g2∧h2)(g_{1}\land h_{1})(g_{2}\land h_{2}). ∎

Corollary 4.18.

Let (A+,Δ)(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+},\Delta) be a monoidal Garside structure such that A+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+} has a ν\nu-structure. Denote by SS its atom set, and by AA its group of fractions. The subgroupoid ℛν​(A)\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle\nu}\!(A)} of ℛ⁡(A)\mathop{\mathcal{R}\!(A)} generated by the ν⁡(X,s)\nu(X,s) is a standard parabolic subgroupoid of ℛ⁡(A)\mathop{\mathcal{R}\!(A)}. Furthermore, Let 𝒜ν\mathcal{A}^{\nu} denote the subgraph of 𝒜\mathcal{A} with the same vertex set and whose edges are the ν⁡(X,s)\nu(X,s). Let RνR^{\nu} be the set of relations of type (3) that appear in Theorem 4.14. Then ⟨𝒜ν,ℛν⟩\langle\mathcal{A}^{\nu},\mathcal{R}^{\nu}\rangle is a presentation of ℛν​(A)\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle\nu}\!(A)} as a groupoid.

Proof.

We recall that the notion of a parabolic subcategory has been introduced in Definition 3.1. We only need to prove that ℛ+ν​(A+)\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+\nu}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})} is a parabolic subcategory of ℛ+​(𝒞)\mathop{\mathcal{R^{\scriptscriptstyle+}}\!(\mathcal{C})} and that ⟨𝒜ν,ℛν⟩\langle\mathcal{A}^{\nu},\mathcal{R}^{\nu}\rangle is a presentation of ℛ+ν​(A+)\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+\nu}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})} as a category. Let AX+A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+} be a parabolic subcategory of A+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+} with ΔX\Delta_{X} as Garside element. The lattice ℛ+ν​(A+)AX+→⋅\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+\nu}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}_{A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\to\cdot} is a sublattice of ℛ+​(A+)AX+→⋅\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}_{A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\to\cdot} by Lemma 4.17. For similar reason, ℛ+ν​(A+)⋅→AX+\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+\nu}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}_{\cdot\to A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}} is a sublattice of ℛ+​(A+)⋅→AX+\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}_{\cdot\to A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}}. By definition [Δ]​(AX+)[\Delta](A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}) is equal to Δ\Delta and we can decompose Δ\Delta as a product ΔX​∇X\Delta_{X}\nabla_{X}. Clearly, ∇X\nabla_{X} lies in ℛ+​(A+)AX+→⋅\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}_{A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\to\cdot}. As AX+A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+} is a parabolic submonoid, no element of XX can left-divides ∇X\nabla_{X}. This implies that ∇X\nabla_{X} lies in ℛ+ν​(A+)AX+→⋅\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+\nu}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}_{A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\to\cdot}. We claim that the equalities

[1,∇X]ℛ+​(A+)=[1,Δ]ℛ+​(A+)⋂ℛ+ν​(A+)AX+→⋅=Δ∧ℛ+ν​(A+)AX+→⋅[1,\nabla_{X}]_{\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}}=[1,\Delta]_{\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}}\bigcap\ {\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+\nu}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}}_{A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\to\cdot}=\Delta\land{\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+\nu}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}}_{A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\to\cdot}

hold. This proves that ℛ+ν​(A+)\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+\nu}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})} is a parabolic subcategory of ℛ+​(𝒞)\mathop{\mathcal{R^{\scriptscriptstyle+}}\!(\mathcal{C})}. Indeed, this equalities are direct consequences of Lemma 4.17: assume gg lie in ℛ+ν​(A+)AX+→⋅{\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+\nu}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}}_{A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\to\cdot} and assume it belongs to [1,Δ]ℛ+​(A+)[1,\Delta]_{\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}}. Write g=g1​g2g=g_{1}g_{2} with g1g_{1} in QZ(AX+)\mathop{\rm QZ}(A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}) and g2g_{2} in ℛ+ν​(A+)AX+→⋅\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+\nu}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}_{A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\to\cdot}. By Lemma 4.17, g1g_{1} and g2g_{2} left-divide ΔX\Delta_{X} and ∇X\nabla_{X}, respectively, and g1=1g_{1}=1 if and only gg left-divides ∇X\nabla_{X}. ∎

We recall that in the case of an Artin-Tits group AA with SS as a generating set, every subset TT of SS generates a standard parabolic subgroup with TT as atom set. In this particular case, we can precise the statement of the Theorem 4.14.

Proposition 4.19.

Let (A+,Δ)(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+},\Delta) be a monoidal Garside structure such that A+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+} is an Artin-Tits monoid of spherical type. Denote by SS its atom set and by AA its associated Artin-Tits group. Assume that XX is a non empty subset of SS and let s,ts,t lie in S−XS-X and be distinct. Then ν⁡(X,s)∨ν⁡(X,t)\nu(X,s)\lor\nu(X,t) has exactly two representing path in the free category 𝒞⁡(𝒜)\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{A}). One begins with ν⁡(X,s)\nu(X,s) and the other with ν⁡(X,t)\nu(X,t).

Proof.

One has ν⁡(X,s)=ΔX−1​ΔX∪{s}\nu(X,s)=\Delta_{X}^{-1}\Delta_{X\cup\{s\}} and ν⁡(X,t)=ΔX−1​ΔX∪{t}\nu(X,t)=\Delta_{X}^{-1}\Delta_{X\cup\{t\}} (cf. Example 3.14). Therefore, ν⁡(X,s)∨ν⁡(X,t)\nu(X,s)\lor\nu(X,t) is equal to ΔX−1​ΔX∪{s,t}\Delta_{X}^{-1}\Delta_{X\cup\{s,t\}} and, in particular, ΔX​(ν⁡(X,s)∨ν⁡(X,t))\Delta_{X}(\nu(X,s)\lor\nu(X,t)) is equal to ΔX∪{s,t}\Delta_{X\cup\{s,t\}}, which is a simple element of A+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+} (c.f. Definition 2.5). Consider in 𝒞⁡(𝒜)\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{A}) a representing path ν(Y0,s0)ν(Y1,s1)⋯ν(Yk,sk)\nu(Y_{0},s_{0})\nu(Y_{1},s_{1})\cdots\nu(Y_{k},s_{k}) of ν⁡(X,s)∨ν⁡(X,t)\nu(X,s)\lor\nu(X,t) such that Y0=XY_{0}=X and s0=ss_{0}=s. Given YiY_{i} and sis_{i}, the set Yi+1Y_{i+1} is uniquely defined by the equality Yi​ν​(Yi,si)=ν⁡(Yi,si)​Yi+1Y_{i}\nu(Y_{i},s_{i})=\nu(Y_{i},s_{i})Y_{i+1}. We can write

ΔX(ν(X,s)∨ν(X,t))=ΔY0∪{s0}ν(Y1,s1)⋯ν(Yk,sk)=\hfil\displaystyle\Delta_{X}(\nu(X,s)\lor\nu(X,t))=\Delta_{Y_{0}\cup\{s_{0}\}}\nu(Y_{1},s_{1})\cdots\nu(Y_{k},s_{k})=\hfill
ν(Y0,s0)ΔY1∪{s1}ν(Y2,s2)⋯ν(Yk,sk)=ν(Y0,s0)⋯ν(Yk−1,sk−1)ΔYk∪{sk}.\hfil\displaystyle\hfill\nu(Y_{0},s_{0})\Delta_{Y_{1}\cup\{s_{1}\}}\nu(Y_{2},s_{2})\cdots\nu(Y_{k},s_{k})=\nu(Y_{0},s_{0})\cdots\nu(Y_{k-1},s_{k-1})\Delta_{Y_{k}\cup\{s_{k}\}}.

Now it is well-known that the simple elements of an Artin-Tits monoid are square free: no representing word of a simple element has a square of an element of SS as a subfactor. This implies that for every 1≤i≤k1\leq i\leq k, the element sis_{i} is uniquely defined by the two conditions si∈S∪{s,t}s_{i}\in S\cup\{s,t\} and si∉{si−1}∪Yi−1s_{i}\not\in\{s_{i-1}\}\cup Y_{i-1}. Thus, there is a unique representing path of ν⁡(X,s)∨ν⁡(X,t)\nu(X,s)\lor\nu(X,t) in 𝒞⁡(𝒜)\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{A}) that starts with ν⁡(X,s)\nu(X,s). Similarly, there is a unique representing path of ν⁡(X,s)∨ν⁡(X,t)\nu(X,s)\lor\nu(X,t) in 𝒞⁡(𝒜)\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{A}) that starts with ν⁡(X,t)\nu(X,t). ∎

4.3. Weak Garside group

In [3], Bessis defined a weak Garside group to be a group that is isomorphic to some vertex group 𝒞x→x\mathcal{C}_{x\to x} of a Garside groupoid 𝒞\mathcal{C}. Clearly a Garside group is a weak Garside group, but there is no obvious general reason for a weak Garside group to be a Garside group [3]. In this section, we consider a Garside group AA with a ν\nu-function and the subgroup GG of some vertex group ℛ⁡(A)AX→AX\mathop{\mathcal{R}\!(A)}_{A_{X}\to A_{X}} that is generated by the atoms of ℛ⁡(A)\mathop{\mathcal{R}\!(A)} that belong to ℛ⁡(A)AX→AX\mathop{\mathcal{R}\!(A)}_{A_{X}\to A_{X}}. Under some assumptions that hold in the case of an Artin-Tits group of spherical type, we prove (cf. Theorem 4.21) that GG is a Garside group. This section is inspired by [6, Theorem B].

We still assume that (A+,Δ)(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+},\Delta) is monoidal Garside structure such that A+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+} has a ν\nu-structure. We still denote by SS and AA the atom set and the group of fractions of A+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}, respectively. For all the section, we fix a standard parabolic subgroup AXA_{X} of AA. We set

SH(X)={νX(s)∣s∈S;νX(s)∈ℛ⁡(A)AX→AX}.{\mathop{\rm SH}}(X)=\{\nu_{X}(s)\mid s\in S\ ;\ \nu_{X}(s)\in{\mathop{\mathcal{R}\!(A)}}_{A_{X}\to A_{X}}\}.

Following [6], we call the elements of SH(X){\mathop{\rm SH}}(X) the shakers of AXA_{X}. It is immediate that the set of shakers SH(X){\mathop{\rm SH}}(X) is equal to {ν~X(s)∣s∈S;ν~X(s)∈ℛ⁡(A)AX→AX}\{\tilde{\nu}_{X}(s)\mid s\in S\ ;\ \tilde{\nu}_{X}(s)\in{\mathop{\mathcal{R}\!(A)}}_{A_{X}\to A_{X}}\}. There is two kinds of shakers, namely the τ⁡(X,s)\tau(X,s) and the ν⁡(X,s)\nu(X,s); in the sequel, we denote by SHν(X){\mathop{\rm SH}}^{\nu}(X) the set {νX​(s)∈SH(X)∣νX​(s)=ν⁡(X,s)}\{\nu_{X}(s)\in{\mathop{\rm SH}}(X)\mid\nu_{X}(s)=\nu(X,s)\}, which is equal to the set {ν~X​(t)∈SH(X)∣ν~X​(t)=ν~​(X,t)}\{\tilde{\nu}_{X}(t)\in{\mathop{\rm SH}}(X)\mid\tilde{\nu}_{X}(t)=\tilde{\nu}(X,t)\}. Furthermore, we denote by sh(X)\mathop{\rm sh}(X) and by sh~⁡(X)\mathop{\widetilde{\rm sh}}(X) the sets νX−1​(SH(X))\nu_{X}^{-1}({\mathop{\rm SH}}(X)) and ν~X−1​(SH(X))\tilde{\nu}_{X}^{-1}({\mathop{\rm SH}}(X)) respectively. There is no reason to expect that sh~⁡(X)=sh(X)\mathop{\widetilde{\rm sh}}(X)=\mathop{\rm sh}(X) in general. Similarly, we set shν(X)=νX−1​(SHν(X))\mathop{\rm sh}^{\nu}(X)=\nu_{X}^{-1}({\mathop{\rm SH}}^{\nu}(X)) and sh~ν⁡(X)=ν~X−1​(SHν(X))\mathop{\widetilde{\rm sh}}^{\nu}(X)=\tilde{\nu}_{X}^{-1}({\mathop{\rm SH}}^{\nu}(X)).

Finally, in the sequel we extend the notation previously used for parabolic submonoids and parabolic subgroups: for every subset XX of A+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}, we denote by AX+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{X} and AXA_{X} the submonoid of A+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+} and the subgroup of AA, respectively, generated by XX. Below, we consider ASH(X)+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{\mathop{\rm SH}(X)} and ASHν(X)+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{{\mathop{\rm SH}}^{\nu}(X)}, which are submonoids of ℛ+​(A+)AX+→AX+\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}_{A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\to A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}}.

Lemma 4.20.

Assume Ash(X)+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{\mathop{\rm sh}(X)} is a parabolic submonoid of A+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}, and denote by Δsh(X)\Delta_{\mathop{\rm sh}(X)} its Garside element. Then,
(i) the elements of SH(X){\mathop{\rm SH}}(X) belong to Ash(X)+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{\mathop{\rm sh}(X)}.
(ii) One has ℛ+​(A+)AX+→⋅∩A+sh(X)=A+SH(X)\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}_{A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\to\cdot}\cap\ A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{\mathop{\rm sh}(X)}=A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{\mathop{\rm SH}(X)}, and every atom of ℛ+​(A+)\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})} that appears in any decomposition of Δsh(X)\Delta_{\mathop{\rm sh}(X)} as a product of atoms in ℛ+​(A+)AX+→⋅\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}_{A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\to\cdot} belongs to SH(X){\mathop{\rm SH}}(X).
(iii) One has ℛ+ν​(A+)AX+→⋅∩A+shν(X)=A+SH(X)ν\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+\nu}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}_{A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\to\cdot}\cap\ A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{\mathop{\rm sh}^{\nu}(X)}=A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{\mathop{\rm SH}(X)^{\nu}}. Write Δsh(X)=ΔX​∇X\Delta_{\mathop{\rm sh}(X)}=\Delta_{X}\nabla_{X}. Then ∇X\nabla_{X} belongs to ASH(X)ν+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{\mathop{\rm SH}(X)^{\nu}}, and every atom of ℛ+ν​(A+)\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+\nu}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})} that appears in any decomposition of ∇(X)\nabla(X) in ℛ+ν​(A+)AX+→⋅\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+\nu}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}_{A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\to\cdot} as a product of atoms belongs to SHν(X){\mathop{\rm SH}}^{\nu}(X).

Proof.

(i) All the elements of sh(X)\mathop{\rm sh}(X) left-divide Δsh(X)\Delta_{\mathop{\rm sh}(X)}, which lies in ℛ+​(A+)AX+→⋅\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}_{A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\to\cdot}. Then, by the defining properties of the ν\nu-structure, it follows that the elements of SH(X)\mathop{\rm SH}(X) left divides Δsh(X)\Delta_{\mathop{\rm sh}(X)}. But Ash(X)+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{\mathop{\rm sh}(X)} is a parabolic submonoid, therefore all the elements of SH(X)\mathop{\rm SH}(X) belong to Ash(X)+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{\mathop{\rm sh}(X)}.
(ii) The set ASH(X)+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{\mathop{\rm SH}(X)} is included in ℛ+​(A+)AX+→⋅∩A+sh(X)\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}_{A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\to\cdot}\cap\ A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{\mathop{\rm sh}(X)} by (i)(i). Conversely, consider an element gg of A+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+} which lies in ℛ+​(A+)AX+→⋅∩A+sh(X)\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}_{A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\to\cdot}\cap\ A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{\mathop{\rm sh}(X)} and choose an arbitrary decomposition νY0(s0)νY1(s1)⋯νYk(sk)\nu_{Y_{0}}(s_{0})\nu_{Y_{1}}(s_{1})\cdots\nu_{Y_{k}}(s_{k}) of gg in ℛ+​(A+)AX+→⋅\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}_{A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\to\cdot} (where Y0=XY_{0}=X). By definition of a ν\nu-structure, we can assume without restriction that each sis_{i} left-divides νYi​(si)\nu_{Y_{i}}(s_{i}); otherwise, if we consider si′s^{\prime}_{i} that left-divides νYi​(si)\nu_{Y_{i}}(s_{i}), then we have νYi​(si′)=νYi​(si)\nu_{Y_{i}}(s^{\prime}_{i})=\nu_{Y_{i}}(s_{i}). The assumption that Ash(X)+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{\mathop{\rm sh}(X)} is a parabolic submonoid implies that all the sis_{i} belong to Ash(X)+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{\mathop{\rm sh}(X)}. Therefore, we get step-by-step that all the YiY_{i} are equal to XX. Then gg belongs to ASH(X)+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{\mathop{\rm SH}(X)}. If we applied the above argument to g=Δsh(X)g=\Delta_{\mathop{\rm sh}(X)} we get the second part of (i​i)(ii).
(iii) The element ΔX\Delta_{X} belongs to QZ(AX+)\mathop{\rm QZ}(A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}) and no element of XX can left-divides ∇X\nabla_{X}. Indeed, if an ss in SS left-divides ∇X\nabla_{X}, then ΔX​s\Delta_{X}s is a simple element of A+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+} and therefore cannot lie in AX+A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}. Then, ∇X\nabla_{X} lies in ASH(X)ν+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{\mathop{\rm SH}(X)^{\nu}} (cf. Lemma 4.17(i)(i)) and the atoms of ℛ+ν​(A+)\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+\nu}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})} that appears in any decomposition of ∇(X)\nabla(X) belongs to SHν(X){\mathop{\rm SH}}^{\nu}(X). ∎

Theorem 4.21.

Let (A+,Δ)(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+},\Delta) be a monoidal Garside structure such that A+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+} has a ν\nu-structure. Denote by SS its atom set and by AA its associated Garside group. Let AX+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{X} be a parabolic submonoid of A+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+} such that sh(X)=sh~⁡(X)\mathop{\rm sh}(X)=\mathop{\widetilde{\rm sh}}(X). If the monoid Ash(X)+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{\mathop{\rm sh}(X)} is a parabolic submonoid of A+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+} whose Garside element is denoted by Δsh(X)\Delta_{\mathop{\rm sh}(X)}, then
(i) the subgroup ASH(X)A_{{\mathop{\rm SH}}(X)} is a standard parabolic subgroup of the groupoid ℛ⁡(A)\mathop{\mathcal{R}\!(A)} with AXA_{X} as unique object. In particular, ASH(X)A_{{\mathop{\rm SH}}(X)} is a Garside group. The Garside element of ASH(X)+A_{\mathop{\rm SH}(X)}^{\scriptscriptstyle+} is Δsh(X)\Delta_{\mathop{\rm sh}(X)} and its atom set is SH(X){\mathop{\rm SH}}(X).
(ii) Write Δsh(X)=ΔX​∇X\Delta_{\mathop{\rm sh}(X)}=\Delta_{X}\nabla_{X}. The subgroup ASHν(X)A_{{\mathop{\rm SH}}^{\nu}(X)} of AA is a (standard) parabolic subgroup of ASH(X)A_{{\mathop{\rm SH}}(X)} with ∇X\nabla_{X} for Garside element, and

ASH(X)=QZ(Ash(X))⋊ASHν(X).A_{{\mathop{\rm SH}}(X)}=\mathop{\rm QZ}(A_{\mathop{\rm sh}(X)})\rtimes A_{{\mathop{\rm SH}}^{\nu}(X)}.
Proof.

(i)(i) The element Δsh(X)\Delta_{\mathop{\rm sh}(X)} belongs to ASH(X)+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{{\mathop{\rm SH}}(X)} and we have

[1AX+,Δsh(X)]ℛ+​(A+)⊆[1AX+,Δ]ℛ+​(A+)∩ASH(X)+⊆(Δ∧Ash(X)+)∩ℛ+​(A+)AX+→⋅\hfil\displaystyle[1_{A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}},\Delta_{\mathop{\rm sh}(X)}]_{\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}}\subseteq[1_{A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}},\Delta]_{\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}}\cap A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{{\mathop{\rm SH}}(X)}\subseteq\left(\Delta\wedge A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{\mathop{\rm sh}(X)}\right)\cap{\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}}_{A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\to\cdot}\hfill
⊆(Δsh(X)∧Ash(X)+)∩ℛ+​(A+)AX+→⋅⊆[1AX+,Δsh(X)]ℛ+​(A+).\hfil\displaystyle\hfill\subseteq\left(\Delta_{{\mathop{\rm sh}}(X)}\wedge A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{\mathop{\rm sh}(X)}\right)\cap{\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}}_{A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\to\cdot}\subseteq[1_{A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}},\Delta_{\mathop{\rm sh}(X)}]_{\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}}.

The first inclusion follows from Lemma 4.20(i​i)(ii), and the third one from the fact that AX+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{X} be a parabolic submonoid of A+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}. By Lemma 4.20(i​i)(ii), we also get that ASH(X)+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{{\mathop{\rm SH}}(X)} is a sublattice of ℛ+​(A+)AX+→⋅\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}_{A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\to\cdot} for the left-divisibility: let gg and hh belong to ASH(X)+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{{\mathop{\rm SH}}(X)}, then their gcd and their lcm for the left-divisibility lie in Ash(X)+A_{{\mathop{\rm sh}}(X)}^{\scriptscriptstyle+} because the latter is a parabolic submonoid of A+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}. But, they also lie in ℛ+​(A+)AX+→⋅\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}_{A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\to\cdot}. Then, by Lemma 4.20(i​i)(ii), they lie in ASH(X)+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{{\mathop{\rm SH}}(X)}, and they are common divisor and common multiple, respectively, of gg and hh in Ash(X)+A_{{\mathop{\rm sh}}(X)}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}. Since we assume sh(X)=sh~⁡(X)\mathop{\rm sh}(X)=\mathop{\widetilde{\rm sh}}(X), by symmetry, ASH(X)+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{{\mathop{\rm SH}}(X)} is a sublattice of ℛ+​(A+)⋅→AX+\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}_{\cdot\to A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}} for the right-divisibility.
(i​i)(ii) We have to prove that ASHν(X)+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{{\mathop{\rm SH}}^{\nu}(X)} is a parabolic submonoid of ASH(X)+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{{\mathop{\rm SH}}(X)}, with ∇X\nabla_{X} as Garside element. This is a consequence of Lemma 4.20(i​i​i)(iii) and 4.17 with a proof similar to (i​i)(ii). It is clear that ASHν(X)+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{{\mathop{\rm SH}}^{\nu}(X)} normalizes QZ+(Ash(X))\mathop{\rm QZ}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}(A_{\mathop{\rm sh}(X)}) and both subgroups generate ASH(X)A_{{\mathop{\rm SH}}(X)}. Finally, we have a semi-direct product because the submonoids QZ+(Ash(X))\mathop{\rm QZ}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}(A_{\mathop{\rm sh}(X)}) and ASHν(X)+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{{\mathop{\rm SH}}^{\nu}(X)} are parabolic with a trivial intersection. Indeed, the left greedy normal of every element in the intersection of the parabolic subgroups QZ(Ash(X))\mathop{\rm QZ}(A_{\mathop{\rm sh}(X)}) and ASHν(X)A_{{\mathop{\rm SH}}^{\nu}(X)} has to be trivial. ∎

In order to state the next result, we recall that an Artin-Tits group of spherical type is said to be indecomposable when it is not the direct product of two of its proper standard parabolic subgroups.

Proposition 4.22.

Let (A+,Δ)(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+},\Delta) be a monoidal Garside structure such that A+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+} is an Artin-Tit monoid of spherical type, with SS as set of atoms and AA as associated Artin-Tits group. Assume that XX is a subset of SS. The subgroup ASH(X)A_{{\mathop{\rm SH}}(X)} is an Artin-Tits group of spherical type with SH(X){\mathop{\rm SH}}(X) as associated atom set. In particular, if s,ts,t are distinct in S−XS-X, the associated Relation (3) of the presentation of ℛ+​(A+)\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})} stated in Theorem 4.14 is

ν(X,t)ν(X,s)ν(X,t)⋯⏟MX,s,t​t​e​r​m​s=ν(X,s)ν(X,t)ν(X,s)⋯⏟MX,s,t​t​e​r​m​s\underbrace{\nu(X,t)\nu(X,s)\nu(X,t)\cdots}_{M_{X,s,t}\ terms}=\underbrace{\nu(X,s)\nu(X,t)\nu(X,s)\cdots}_{M_{X,s,t}\ terms}

for some positive integer MX,s,tM_{X,s,t}. When ASA_{S} is indecomposable with #​S≥3\#S\geq 3, the subgroups ASH(X)A_{{\mathop{\rm SH}}(X)} of AA where X⊂SX\subset S are classified by the tables of relations R2 of [6, Appendix 5].

Proof.

By Theorem 4.21, we know that ASH(X)A_{{\mathop{\rm SH}}(X)} is a Garside group with SH(X){\mathop{\rm SH}}(X) as associated atom set. Now, consider the decomposition ν(X,s)ν(Y1,s1)⋯ν(Yk,sk)\nu(X,s)\nu(Y_{1},s_{1})\cdots\nu(Y_{k},s_{k}) of ν⁡(X,s)∨ν⁡(X,t)\nu(X,s)\lor\nu(X,t) that starts with ν⁡(X,s)\nu(X,s) in 𝒞⁡(𝒜)\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{A}) (cf. Proposition 4.19). By assumption, Y1=XY_{1}=X. By the argument of the proof of Proposition 4.19, we get s1=ts_{1}=t, then Y2=XY_{2}=X, and step-by-step that ν⁡(X,s)∨ν⁡(X,t)=ν(X,s)ν(X,t)ν(X,s)⋯⏟k​ terms\nu(X,s)\lor\nu(X,t)=\underbrace{\nu(X,s)\nu(X,t)\nu(X,s)\cdots}_{k\textrm{ terms}}. Similarly ν⁡(X,s)∨ν⁡(X,t)=ν(X,t)ν(X,s)ν(X,t)⋯⏟ℓ​ terms\nu(X,s)\lor\nu(X,t)=\underbrace{\nu(X,t)\nu(X,s)\nu(X,t)\cdots}_{\ell\textrm{ terms}}. Finally, k=ℓk=\ell because otherwise we could decompose ν⁡(X,s)∨ν⁡(X,t)\nu(X,s)\lor\nu(X,t)~ as a product w1​(ν⁡(X,s)∨ν⁡(X,t))​w2w_{1}(\nu(X,s)\lor\nu(X,t))w_{2} with (w1,w2)≠(1,1)(w_{1},w_{2})\neq(1,1), which is impossible. Then ASH(X)A_{{\mathop{\rm SH}}(X)} is an Artin-Tits group of spherical type with SH(X){\mathop{\rm SH}}(X) as associated atom set. The proof of the remaining is a case by case computation, which is the same as in [6]. ∎

4.4. Semi-direct product

Theorem 4.21 of the previous section claims that the group ASH(X)A_{{\mathop{\rm SH}}(X)} is a semi-direct product of two of its subgroups. In order to established that result, we use Lemma 4.17 (i)(i). If we were dealing with groups instead of categories in the latter, we would have use the notion of a group semi-direct product in order to state it. The notion of a semi-direct product of categories is not so easy to defined, even though one can find a definition in [12], or more recently in [23]. The notion of a Zappa-Szép product, as covered in [5], appears as more natural.

Definition 4.23 (Zappa-Szép product).

[5, Lemma 3.2 and 3.9] Let 𝒞\mathcal{C} be a category and 𝒟,𝒟′\mathcal{D},\mathcal{D}^{\prime} be two subcategories of 𝒞\mathcal{C}. We say that 𝒞\mathcal{C} is an (internal) Zappa-Szép product of 𝒟\mathcal{D} and 𝒟′\mathcal{D}^{\prime} if every morphism gg of 𝒞\mathcal{C} can be uniquely decomposed as a product g1​g2g_{1}g_{2} where g1g_{1} is a morphism of 𝒟\mathcal{D} and g2g_{2} is a morphism of 𝒟′\mathcal{D}^{\prime}. In this case, we write 𝒞=𝒟⋈𝒟′\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{D}\bowtie\mathcal{D}^{\prime}.

Then, Lemma 4.17(i)(i) claims that ℛ+​(A+)=𝒬𝒵+(A)⋈ℛ+ν​(A+)\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}=\mathcal{QZ}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}(A)\bowtie\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+\nu}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})} where 𝒬​𝒵+​(A)\mathcal{QZ}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}(A) be the totally disconnected category whose objects are the parabolic submonoids of A+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+} and whose vertex monoid at AX+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{X} is QZ+(AX+)\mathop{\rm QZ}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{X}). Clearly, in our context, we have more than a Zappa-Szép product. Let us introduce the following definition:

Definition 4.24 (Semi-direct product).

Let 𝒞\mathcal{C} be a category and 𝒟,𝒟′\mathcal{D},\mathcal{D}^{\prime} be two subcategories of 𝒞\mathcal{C} such that 𝒞=𝒟⋈𝒟′\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{D}\bowtie\mathcal{D}^{\prime}. Assume 𝒟\mathcal{D} is equal to a totally disconnected category that is the union of its vertex monoids 𝒟x→x{\mathcal{D}}_{x\to x}. We say that 𝒞\mathcal{C} is a semi-direct product of 𝒟\mathcal{D} and 𝒟′\mathcal{D}^{\prime} when for every gg in 𝒟′x→y{\mathcal{D}^{\prime}}_{x\to y} one has 𝒟x→x​g=g​𝒟y→y{\mathcal{D}}_{x\to x}g=g{\mathcal{D}}_{y\to y}. In this case, we write 𝒞=𝒟⋊𝒟′\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{D}\rtimes\mathcal{D}^{\prime}.

So, for instance one has ℛ+​(A+)=𝒬𝒵+(A)⋊ℛ+ν​(A+)\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}=\mathcal{QZ}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}(A)\rtimes\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+\nu}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}. This definition extends the standard definition of a semi-direct product of monoids, and is a special case of the definition considered in [23]. We finish this article with the following result which generalizes [15, Prop. 4] and provides a nice description of the connection between the standard parabolic subgroups of a Garside group.

Theorem 4.25.

Let (A+,Δ)(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+},\Delta) be a monoidal Garside structure such that A+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+} has a ν\nu-structure. Denote by AA the group of fractions of A+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}.
(i) Let 𝒬​𝒵​(A)\mathcal{QZ}(A) be the totally disconnected groupoid whose objects are the parabolic subgroups of AA and whose vertex group at AXA_{X} is QZ(AX)\mathop{\rm QZ}(A_{X}). Then,

ℛ⁡(A)=𝒬𝒵(A)⋊ℛν​(A).\mathop{\mathcal{R}\!(A)}=\mathcal{QZ}(A)\rtimes\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle\nu}\!(A)}.

(ii) Let C​o​n​j​(A)Conj(A) be the groupoid whose objects are the parabolic subgroups of AA, whose morphism set C​o​n​j​(A)AX→AYConj(A)_{A_{X}\to A_{Y}} from AXA_{X} to AYA_{Y} is {g∈A∣g−1​AX​g=AY}\{g\in A\mid g^{-1}A_{X}g=A_{Y}\}, and whose composition is the product in AA. Let 𝒫⁡(A)\mathcal{P}(A) be the totally disconnected groupoid whose objects are the parabolic subgroups of AA and whose vertex group at AXA_{X} is AXA_{X}. Then,

Conj(A)=𝒫(A)⋊ℛν​(A).Conj(A)=\mathcal{P}(A)\rtimes\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle\nu}\!(A)}.

Note that C​o​n​j​(A)Conj(A) is the full subgroupoid of 𝒩​⟨A⟩\mathop{\mathcal{N}\langle A\rangle} (see Definition 2.14) whose objects are the parabolic subgroups of AA. Its vertex groups are normalizers of standard parabolic subgroups. This result holds in particular when AA is an Artin-Tits group of spherical type.

Proof.

(i)(i) The unique not obvious fact is that ℛ⁡(A)\mathop{\mathcal{R}\!(A)} is equal to the Zappa-Szép product 𝒬𝒵(A)⋈ℛν​(A)\mathcal{QZ}(A)\bowtie\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle\nu}\!(A)}. This is a consequence of the Zappa-Szép product decomposition of ℛ+​(A+)\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}, since ℛ⁡(A)\mathop{\mathcal{R}\!(A)}, 𝒬​𝒵​(A)\mathcal{QZ}(A) and ℛν​(A)\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle\nu}\!(A)} are the groupoids of fractions of the Garside categories ℛ+​(A+)\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}, 𝒬​𝒵+​(A+)\mathcal{QZ}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}) and ℛ+ν​(A+)\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+\nu}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}, respectively (where 𝒬​𝒵+​(A+)\mathcal{QZ}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}) is the totally disconnected category whose objects are the parabolic submonoids of A+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+} and whose vertex monoid at AX+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{X} is QZ(AX+)\mathop{\rm QZ}(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{X})).
(i​i)(ii) Again the unique not obvious fact is that Conj(A) = 𝒫(A)⋈ℛν​(A)\mathcal{P}(A)\bowtie\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle\nu}\!(A)}. The unicity of the decomposition follows easily from Lemma 4.17(i​i)(ii). Let gg lie in AA such that g−1​AX​g=AYg^{-1}A_{X}g=A_{Y}. We show there exist aa in AXA_{X} and rr in ℛν​(A)AX→AY\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle\nu}\!(A)}_{A_{X}\to A_{Y}} such that g=a​rg=ar. There exists n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} and g1g_{1} in A+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+} such that g=g1​Δ−ng=g_{1}\Delta^{-n}. Furthermore, there exists a parabolic submonoid AZ+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{Z} of A+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+} such that Δn\Delta^{n} belongs to ℛ+​(A+)AY+→AZ+\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}_{A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{Y}\to A^{\scriptscriptstyle+}_{Z}}. In particular, we have g1−1​AX​g1=AZg_{1}^{-1}A_{X}g_{1}=A_{Z}. We can write g1=a1​r1​b1g_{1}=a_{1}r_{1}b_{1} such that a1a_{1} belongs to AX+A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}, b1b_{1} belongs to AZ+A_{Z}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}, no elements of XX left-divides r1r_{1} and no element of ZZ right-divides r1r_{1}. Now, let xx belongs to XX and c−1​zc^{-1}z be the left greedy normal form of r1−1​x​r1r_{1}^{-1}xr_{1} in AA. There exists dd in A+A^{\scriptscriptstyle+} such that x​r1=d​zxr_{1}=dz and r1=d​cr_{1}=dc. Since r1−1​x​r1r_{1}^{-1}xr_{1} belongs to AZA_{Z}, the elements cc and zz belongs to AZ+A_{Z}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}. By the assumption on r1r_{1}, this implies c=1c=1 and r1−1​x​r1=zr_{1}^{-1}xr_{1}=z. Therefore r1​AX+​r1−1r_{1}A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}r_{1}^{-1} is included in AZ+A_{Z}^{\scriptscriptstyle+} and by symmetry, r1​AX+​r1−1=AZ+r_{1}A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}r_{1}^{-1}=A_{Z}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}. Therefore, r1r_{1} lies in ℛ+​(A+)AX+→AZ+\mathop{\mathcal{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\!(A^{\scriptscriptstyle+})}_{A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}\to A_{Z}^{\scriptscriptstyle+}} and we have g=a1​r1​b1​Δ−n=a1​a2​r1​Δ−ng=a_{1}r_{1}b_{1}\Delta^{-n}=a_{1}a_{2}r_{1}\Delta^{-n} with a1​a2a_{1}a_{2} in AX+A_{X}^{\scriptscriptstyle+} and r1​Δ−nr_{1}\Delta^{-n} in ℛ⁡(A)AX→AY\mathop{\mathcal{R}\!(A)}_{A_{X}\to A_{Y}}. Using (i)(i), we are done. ∎
